chapters.content:
I. THE UNFINISHED BETRAYER

Antonio da Vinci, margin of the keeper’s journal

Leonardo da Vinci

Milan, refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie

February 1497

The face opens its eyes before I finish painting them.

I freeze mid-stroke. The pupils are not there. I have not rendered them.

Then comes the slow, sick recognition that the wet umber where the eyes should be is moving, not drying, not settling into the plaster the way fresh pigment is supposed to settle, but stirring like oil on water.

Across the half-painted features a smile begins to assemble itself out of nothing I have laid down.

Maestro.

Not a voice. Pressure. Words shoved against the inside of my skull as though from a hand on the other side of bone.

Maestro. I see you.

My palette knife is in my hand before I have chosen to lift it. The blade goes into the wet pigment, scrapes, gouges, peels back three hours of work in three strokes; burnt umber sprays across the front of my smock and onto the planks of the scaffolding and onto the back of my left wrist. The face goes under the steel. The plaster shows raw beneath, fresh and pale as new bone, scoured clean, and still I can feel her on the other side, pressing with the same patient warmth a child’s palm makes against a window glass on a cold morning.

“Maestro?”

Marco. From below, on the floor of the refectory, where the ordinary world still operates. I turn too fast; the scaffolding shifts; my boot finds a knot in the board where my weight should not be.

I crouch. I reach for the rope.

My hand misses.

The palette knife slides out of my fingers, ricochets off the iron clamp on the next board down, falls again. The drop is long. When the blade strikes the stone flagstones of the refectory the sound that comes back up to me is not the sound a knife should make.

The sound is a bell.

It rings once in the high arched ceiling, holds there a moment longer than physics permits, and dies.

Marco stares at the fallen knife, then up at me. His face has gone the colour of the gesso ground I prepared this morning. His chest rises and does not fall.

“The pigments.” My voice arrives from somewhere outside my body. “Incorrectly ground. Fetch fresh vermilion from the workshop.”

He does not move. His eyes drift toward the place on the wall where the face that was not finished had begun to finish itself, then back to me, then to the fallen knife, then to a spot on the floor a few inches from his boot, anywhere, in fact, except where he is being instructed to look.

“Maestro, the wall…”

“Now, Marco.”

The jar of walnut oil he was carrying is on the flagstones at his feet, slowly tipping. He has not noticed. He sets it down at last with the carefulness of a man handling a relic, crosses himself with his thumb in the old Lombard way, hard and small, the gesture of a man who does not believe in ghosts but has decided this afternoon to hedge, and goes. The heavy door of the refectory closes behind him.

I do not move.

Forty-four years I have carried this body, and lately my knees have begun their old peasant grievance against the weight; but the knees are not the problem this afternoon. The problem is my left hand, which will not stop trembling, which I press flat against my chest to still and which will not be stilled. Below me the palette knife lies where it fell. I cannot make my body climb down to retrieve it.

The refectory is silent.

The kind of silent that has weight. The kind I measured in chapels as a boy, kneeling before the host while the priest raised the bread and the world stopped speaking for the length of his elevation, only without the bread. Without God in it.

The Judas-shaped wound in my wall waits.

When at last I climb down, the descent takes longer than it should. I have done this every day for two years and my body knows every rung, every soft place where the boards creak; today my body has forgotten its own work, and I count the rungs as if they are a stranger’s stairs.

At the bottom the palette knife lies where Marco’s eyes left it. I do not pick it up. I cross to the long view, the place where the great Dominican brothers enter in procession on feast days, where a viewer first sees the Cenacolo whole, and from there the wall finally permits me the geometry of what I have made.

Eleven faces look back at me.

Christ at the centre. His left hand turned up, open: one of you will betray me. His right hand turned down, closed: and the betrayer’s bread is in this dish. The whole composition lives in those two hands, and I painted them across November and most of December knowing that anything anyone says about this wall for a thousand years will begin with the way the left hand opens.

To Christ’s right, Peter lunges with the knife, the one I studied in the meat district along the Naviglio, where I spent three afternoons sketching the wrists of a butcher named Giacomo whose tendons knotted into the specific muscle that pulls a blade across a throat. Peter’s hand on this wall is Giacomo’s hand. Peter does not know it.

Beyond Peter, John has swooned. James the Greater throws his hands up. Thomas raises his single finger toward heaven, his question already forming.

Then the empty space.

The blank shape where Judas Iscariot ought to clutch his thirty silver. A wound in the composition: roughly ten inches by twelve, the dimensions of a face and therefore the dimensions of an absence, the plaster paler than the surrounding wall because it has been scraped seventeen times.

The other apostles ring the table and look at one another, look at Christ, look at the bread and the wine and the slowly forming knife. Their gazes complete a circuit, a closed circle that holds the viewer’s eye inside the painting. Judas would break the circle. Judas is supposed to break the circle.

I move closer than I have come today, close enough that my breath should mist on the cold plaster, would mist if I were breathing.

I am not breathing.

I do not touch the wall. I do not need to.

The plaster is not thick enough to hide this.

I know its thickness. I supervised its construction. Three-quarters of an inch of plaster, then brick, then mortar, then the cloister of the Dominicans, where six monks are at this moment chanting Vespers and have not yet noticed that the wall between us has begun to grow soft.

Seventeen attempts.

The thought goes nowhere. I let it sit.

I have failed at finishing things before. The Adoration sits in Florence, unfinished, a brown ghost of underdrawing waiting for colour I will never lay down. The great bronze horse stands as clay in Ludovico’s courtyard waiting for a casting that the city’s gunmakers want the bronze for instead. The mechanical lion I designed for the French. The diving apparatus. The flying machine. I am a man who begins.

The seventeen Judases are not that kind of unfinishing. The seventeen Judases were finished. Each of them. And then unmade.

The first was too cruel. I gave him the face of a moneylender I had known in Florence, all jaw and appetite, and as the pigment began to dry the eyes shifted under my brush. The cruelty became something I could not paint with. Something that looked back. I scraped it that same afternoon, before the prior arrived to inquire after my progress.

The second was too pious. I tried to imagine Judas as he had been before the betrayal, the boy from Kerioth who had followed a teacher. The face I painted was tender. The pigment had not dried when the tenderness inverted, and the mouth I had given that boy became a mouth I no longer wanted in my refectory after dark.

The third was too young. The fourth too old. The fifth had eyes I could not bear to keep on the wall after sunset.

The sixth was the one I noticed.

The sixth was correct. I rendered the underdrawing in red ochre, laid in the flesh tones with the same technique I had used on Bartholomew, the same pigments, the same brushes, the same hand. The composition demanded a man who had decided. The man I painted had decided. He was ordinary, neither cruel nor tender, neither young nor old, with the calm of a small functionary at his master’s table.

Then the pigment began to dry, and something else rushed to fill the form.

Not my Judas. Another face. Pressing through the plaster from behind the wet pigment, opening within the shape I had outlined, smiling with a mouth that was not the mouth I had given. I scraped him before the smile finished.

Seventeen, now.

Dimmi: how can a face see without eyes?

The question that came to me on the scaffolding this afternoon arrives again, weighted differently at the long view. From here the seventeen attempts compress into a single absence, a door left open in the geometry of my Christ.

Behind me the pigments wait on the shelf where I left them at dawn: malachite for green, lead-tin yellow, azzurro della Magna I bought from a Genoese merchant for more than the monks’ yearly bread, vermilion freshly ground this morning by Marco’s still-thin fingers. The dust motes drift through the slanted afternoon light. The light is doing what light has always done.

Maestro.

Faint. Not in my head this time. In the wall.

You are painting toward the wrong face. He is not in the gospels. He is in the geometry of your own composition.

I do not turn. I do not answer.

Artists return to their masterpieces.

The phrase rises in me without invitation, summoned from somewhere outside my own thinking. I have heard it said, among the masters in Florence, in the bottega gossip, in the way one painter speaks of another at a long dinner he was not invited to. I have not, until this winter, understood it as a sentence of imprisonment.

The voice in the wall waits for me.

I approach the wall.

The afternoon light is leaving. In another hour the refectory will be the colour of unmilled flour, and in another two the colour of the inside of a tomb. I will need lamps if I am to work. I do not intend to work. I do not, in fact, intend to remain in this room. But my feet have brought me to the wall as feet have brought men to confession boxes for fifteen hundred years, and I am, in this small surrendering moment, no different from a man on his knees.

I lift my hand to the plaster.

An inch from the surface, I stop.

The plaster is cold. The refectory is cold. Lombardy in February is the wet cold that settles into the joints of an old building and stays there until April. The plaster is colder than the air around it, which is what plaster should be, but only just.

I press my palm flat against the Judas-space.

Something presses back.

Not heat. Not exactly heat. Pressure: the smallest pressure, an ounce, perhaps less, but present and willed, the pressure a child’s hand makes against a window, the pressure a hand makes against a hand.

You are too kind to him.

Her voice in the wall. No syllables. The shape of words laid against the inside of my skull as if from a hand on the other side of bone.

Your apostles look at one another. They look at Christ. They look at the bread. Their gazes complete a circuit. Your Judas is alone, you have decided who he is before giving him a face. You have left him faceless because you are afraid he will look ordinary.

My palm rests on the plaster. The plaster’s pressure rests on my palm. We are touching.

I have known many men who would betray Christ for thirty silver, she goes on, conversational, the way a fellow craftsman might lean against the bench in the corner of a workshop, and I have collected them. I can give you a face, Maestro. A face the world will recognise.

My hand does not move.

Your bronze horse, Maestro. Fourteen years of bozzetti. The clay is still in Ludovico’s courtyard. Shall I tell you where it will be melted, and by whom, and in what year? Shall I tell you what becomes of the wax models you have shown only to your apprentices? I have read your notebooks, not the ones you keep open on the table, the other ones, the ones you write left-handed in the mirror.

The pressure on my palm steadies, as if she has settled into a more comfortable posture against the inside of the wall, the way a guest settles into a chair offered by a host who has not yet realised the visit will be long.

Set his gaze outward, she says, returning to the business of her commission. Let him meet the viewer’s eyes. Let the betrayal be seen, not hidden among gestures. The composition demands it.

She is correct.

This is the worst thing she has said.

She is correct, and I have known it for weeks, perhaps months, perhaps since the eleventh attempt, the composition demands a face that breaks the circle. It demands a Judas who looks out at the room, who looks at the monks at their meal, who looks at the wealthy donors when they come on feast days to admire what their florins have purchased. The painting requires it. The geometry requires it. I have been pretending otherwise, but I have spent my life understanding geometry, and geometry does not lie.

She has just told me how to finish my masterpiece, and I have just understood that the moment I do, the door opens.

Yes, she says, as if my thought were spoken aloud. Yes. Now we understand each other.

My palm has begun to sweat against the cold plaster. I can feel her fingers on the other side of the wall. They have a shape now. They mirror mine. Five against five. The pressure increases.

“I will not finish his face today.”

I have spoken aloud. My voice is level. How my voice is level, I do not know.

The pressure does not lessen. The pressure becomes thoughtful.

I have time, Maestro.

Her voice has changed. The argument is over. The critic has heard the gallery’s verdict and is unconcerned.

The plaster will dry. And dry plaster, in the end, will take whatever face we agree upon.

I pull my hand away. The pressure releases. The plaster is plaster again, cold and February and three-quarters of an inch thick, with a cloister behind it and six men in it chanting the Office of the dead.

I look down at my hand.

The burnt umber from the scraped face is still on my skin, the smear by the thumb. I scraped it three hours ago. By now the pigment should be cool, tacky, beginning to flake. By now the pigment should not behave.

The pigment is warm.

The door opens. I am still at the wall when Marco returns, my hand still raised in front of me, my palm still warm with what was on the other side of the plaster. He hesitates at the threshold. He is not alone.

“Maestro,” he says. “The Prior.”

Vincenzo Bandello. Prior of Santa Maria delle Grazie, friend of dukes, second cousin to a cardinal, and, for the past two years, the man whose patience I have measured in audiences instead of florins. He is a small, round, methodical Lombard with a face that arranges itself for any conversation by first deciding what kind of conversation it would prefer not to be having. Just now his face has decided that this conversation will be reluctant.

He steps into the refectory. He looks at the scaffolding. He looks at the palette knife on the flagstones, where it has been lying since Marco crossed himself over it half an hour ago. He looks at the Judas-shaped wound on the wall. He does not look at it for long.

“Maestro Leonardo.”

“Prior.”

“The Duke,” he says, in the tone of a man who has been instructed to deliver a message and would prefer the message had been entrusted to a courier, “has asked again.”

“The Duke asks weekly. The Duke is to be commended for his persistence.”

“Maestro.”

“Prior.”

“He has asked,” Bandello says, with a small and careful precision, “whether you would be insulted if he engaged a second hand. A Florentine, from Verrocchio’s old workshop. Lorenzo di Credi, I think, would be the…”

“He would not be insulted on my behalf, Prior. He would be insulting me directly. There is a difference.”

“He understands the difference.”

“And yet he proposes it.”

Bandello’s face acquires the thin smile of a man who has spent a long career mediating disputes between sons-in-law and the saints. “He proposes it, Maestro, because for fourteen months you have given him a wall that is eleven-twelfths of a Last Supper. Mathematically he is correct that we are eleven-twelfths nearer the feast than we were when you began. Theologically he is correct that the eleven-twelfth is not the part that matters.”

The Judas-shape behind him does not move. I am very aware that it does not move. I am very aware that I must remain aware that it does not move.

“Prior. There is no second hand. Not on this wall. Not on this face.”

“Maestro.”

“Not on this face.”

“Forgive me, Maestro. May I ask why the face refuses you?”

He has asked this in four previous audiences. The question has cost him something to keep asking. In each audience I have given a different lie. The composition demands further study. The pigment requires longer drying. The Duke’s choice of subject obliges an unusual treatment. I am running out of lies. I have known for some weeks now that I am running out of lies, and that the Prior knows I know, and that the next audience after this one will not be a polite one.

“The face,” I say, “is a difficult problem.”

“All faces are difficult problems.”

“Not all faces are betrayals.”

He waits for me to continue. I do not. He looks once at the Judas-shape and once at the palette knife, and then, perhaps for the second time in our acquaintance, at me, as if measuring something he is not in the habit of measuring.

“Maestro. If you require additional study, study. The Duke will allow another month. He will not allow another six. You know this. I have told him you know this.” He pauses. “I have also told him I have eaten my breakfast in this refectory for fourteen years, and that in fourteen years I have never once felt cold in this room until this winter. He laughed. I did not.”

He turns to leave. At the door he stops.

“Maestro. The face Christ looks toward. It is not the face you have left blank.”

“Prior?”

He does not answer the question. He goes. Marco follows him out with the apologetic step of an apprentice between two larger weathers, and the door closes behind them.

It is some seconds before I can move again.

When I do, it is to a small wooden chest in the corner where I keep correspondence I will not throw away, and that is where Marco finds me when he comes back a quarter of an hour later, with the courier behind him.

The wax is black.

I take the letter. Marco lingers. The courier turns to go.

“Marco. Go home.”

“Maestro…”

“Go home.”

The handwriting on the address belongs to my father, Ser Piero da Vinci, notary of Florence, who has not written to me in nearly six years and writes now in the small deliberate hand of a man who charges by the legal phrase. I break the seal. I read the letter once. I read it again. I do not feel the news, because the news is more than thirty years old and has only now decided to arrive.

The box has changed.

The thought has the flatness of an entry in a notary’s ledger, which is the only register my father owns. The chest your grandfather left in my keeping, that I was charged to hold shut and to speak of to no one until it should alter, has altered. There is frost on the wax in a warm room. It carries a weight it did not carry. My father’s instruction was plain, and I have kept it more than thirty years against my own wishes: when the box wakes, it goes to Leonardo, and to no one else, and not in Vinci. Come and take this thing out of my house. I would have written it in his voice had he not. He is a man who writes the waking of buried things the way the rest of us write inventories.

I fold the letter. I am to come to Vinci.

I cannot leave Milan now, not with the Judas unfinished and her hand pressing through the wall and the plaster warm where it should be cold. I have a thousand reasons that are not the reason. The reason is that I have spent thirty years not thinking about my grandfather’s box, and the wall has spent three weeks teaching me that I was wrong to stop.

I unlock the chest where I keep what is left of him. Inside, near the top, are seven letters in his hand, the ink gone brown, the paper soft with handling and age. He wrote them to a boy. The last is more than thirty years old. In every one of them, somewhere, he told me he was tired, and that he had something to send when the time was right, and I was a child and did not think to ask what, and then he was in the ground and the time was never right, and I came north and became Leonardo and let the letters go brown in a chest.

I lift the seven letters.

The fourth, from beneath, is not where I left it. It sits closer to the top than I left it, and I have not opened this chest in years.

Someone has moved the letter. I did not move the letter.

I close the chest. I sit on the bench beside it. The shaking has spread to both hands.

Behind me, in the Judas-shaped wound in the wall, the plaster is no longer drying.

The light leaves us slowly. I do not light the lamps. The refectory deepens from afternoon into the colour of unmilled flour, then linen, then the inside of a tomb, and I should go: the monks will come for Vespers in the connecting cloister, and they will hear me alone here in the dark, and the rumours about the Florentine who scrapes his own work each afternoon will become rumours about the Florentine who haunts his own work after dusk.

Rumour I can survive. I do not move.

When I finally rise, my legs have forgotten how to be legs. I cross to the wall by the memory of crossings. The Judas-space is the dimension of a man’s face: ten inches by twelve, perhaps her face, though I do not know if she has a face, do not know if a face is what she is asking me to give her.

I lift my hand to within an inch of the plaster.

The plaster bulges.

So small a movement that for a moment I do not trust my eyes. I have not slept properly in three weeks; I have stopped eating with regularity; I am a man whose eyes have invented many things, the way all painters’ eyes invent things, the way we are paid to invent them. But I have watched plaster dry every day of my working life, and wet plaster does not bulge.

The bulge holds: a swelling no larger than the back of a knuckle, pushed outward toward my waiting palm.

I lay my palm against it. For two heartbeats, the bulge is fingers, five of them, splayed against the inside of the wall, the pads of them pressing through the plaster the way a child presses through a stretched bedsheet. Thumb. Index. Middle. Ring. The little finger curled slightly inward.

I have dissected hands. I know what a hand feels like through a thin barrier. I know the difference between the texture of skin and the texture of plaster. I do not invent this.

I pull my hand away. The bulge subsides.

The fingers were not fingers, I tell myself, and the lie is so transparent that even she does not bother with it.

Maestro.

Soft. Almost gentle. The voice that came up to me on the scaffolding hours ago.

Did you feel my hand?

I do not answer.

The door is in the wall.

The thought arrives in the chamber of my own skull, and I cannot say whether I have thought it or whether she has placed it there. The distinction has stopped meaning what it should.

I turn to leave. I get three steps. My hand is on the iron handle of the refectory door, and I am going to walk out of this room and not return tonight, possibly never return alone after dark, possibly never return at all.

I look back.

In the Judas-space, where there should be only scraped plaster in the failing light, there is a smile, wide, pleasant, patient enough to require no patience. The smile of a guest at a dinner arranged for the guest’s benefit. It is there for the half-second I look at it, and then it is plaster again. Plaster, wet plaster, nothing. The light is failing. My eyes are tired. I have not slept. The smile was not a smile. The fingers were not fingers.

I open the door. I step into the cloister. I close the door behind me and turn the key, and the iron clicks into place with the sound of a thing being made certain.

I stand outside the door for a long time. The monks pass on their way to choir. They nod. The Prior is among them now, he has not changed his coat since the afternoon, and he looks at me a moment longer than the others. He does not stop. He has a long memory for slights and a longer memory for unpaid commissions, and the next audience between us will not be polite.

When the cloister is empty, I speak aloud. The vault catches my voice and holds it as the refectory caught the bell of the fallen palette knife.

“I will go to Vinci.”

II. THE LITTLE DEVIL

“Every keeper inherits two things. The pigments. And the proof that someone before him failed.”

Antonio da Vinci, keeper’s journal, undated page

Leonardo da Vinci

Leonardo’s workshop, Corte Vecchia, Milan

Late February 1497

The road to Vinci took four days, the road back another four, and I have been in Milan two more. The cart that brought the box is in the stable behind the Corte Vecchia, the driver paid, the donkey unhitched and led to feed. The box itself sits on the workbench in the upper room of my workshop, where I placed it perhaps fifteen minutes ago, and where I have not stopped looking at it since.

The workshop is cold. Eighteen months ago this room would have held seven apprentices and two journeymen: the noise of bronze molds being inverted for the great horse, the smell of fresh-grated charcoal, the constant low argument over who had borrowed whose chisel. Today there is one brazier burning low and one lamp lit beyond what the high window provides. The bronze horse molds have gone into the cellar where Ludovico’s men carted them after the Duke decided the bronze was wanted for cannon-stock. The apprentices have been reassigned to the Castello, where Ludovico is building rooms for guests who will never come because the French are coming first.

I have lit the brazier myself, and laid the bread Marco left for me on a stool I am not sitting on. The shop smells of dust on cold linseed, of the inside of a cabinet that has not been opened in a season.

The box smells of nothing.

I am aware of that. A box that has held seven sealed vials of pigment, plus a journal, plus a wrapped panel, plus whatever else my grandfather left for me, should smell of something: wood, wax, the slow incense of old paper. This box smells of nothing.

There was no one to bury. My grandfather has lain in the churchyard at Vinci more than thirty years, in the plot beside my grandmother and the empty stones for the children who did not live to be named. I stood at the grave a while in the February rain. The stone has the soft edges stone gets in thirty years of weather. I was twelve the last time I stood on that ground, the autumn the leaves came down the colour of old coins, and I held the cord they lowered him by, and I did not understand then that the family was not only burying a man but closing a door they were all relieved to be shut of.

My father kept the box closed the whole while I was in Vinci, the way he has kept it closed for thirty years. He gave it to me only when I was leaving, on the road outside town, where he could be sure no one in the family would see it change hands.

“It goes to you,” he said. “Only to you. Not in Vinci. He was very clear, at the end, and I have kept his clarity longer than I have kept anything of my own. Take it out of my house, Leonardo, and do not write to me of it again.”

He had stood there in his good wool, the rain at his collar, his face arranged for a conversation he had rehearsed for thirty years and prayed he would never have to give. I waited for him to say more. He did not. I have not asked my father what he knew. He has not offered.

I sit on a stool. The bread is hard, cold to the touch. I do not eat it. I have not opened the box.

For fifteen minutes my hand has not crossed the small distance between my lap and the lid. There is a brass hook on the lid that needs to be lifted to release the latch. The hook is perhaps the length of my smallest finger. I cannot make my hand close on it.

“You are back.”

The voice from the room below. Salai. Up the stairs in eleven quick strides, the way only Salai climbs stairs, every step half a stride longer than it should be. He arrives in the doorway with a small loaf of dark bread tucked under one arm, a wedge of pecorino in waxed paper, a bowl of olives glistening from their oil, and half a flask of wine he probably did not pay for.

Seventeen years old. Curls he refuses to cut. The boy who climbed those stairs at ten and never quite left.

He takes in the room in two passes. The first pass: the cold brazier, the unlit lamps, the stool with the untouched bread on it, my hands in my lap. The second pass: the box.

He does not ask about the box.

He sets the food on the bench beside it. He cuts the loaf with the knife I have not seen him return to the kitchen, ever, in seven years. He pushes a piece across the wood without looking up.

“Eat.”

“I am not hungry.”

“So either you are lying about not being hungry, or you are lying about working. Either way you owe me an answer when you finish chewing.”

I take the bread.

He cuts the pecorino with the same knife and arranges the olives in a careful line along the rim of the bowl, smallest to largest, as if presentation might persuade me. He pours wine into the single cup we keep on this bench, drinks half of it, and pushes the rest to me.

“You were gone ten days.”

“Four there. Two at Vinci. Four back.”

“You never told me your grandfather had left you anything.”

“I did not know he had, until my father wrote that it had started to wake.”

Salai considers this, choosing not to ask the question he is choosing not to ask. He has been told, twice in his life, things about the da Vinci dead that he did not ask to be told. The first time he asked questions. The second time he did not. He has learned that the da Vinci dead are not the kind one asks about, and that my grandfather, thirty years buried, is somehow the least dead of all of them.

The bread is good. I had not known I was this hungry. I had not known anything about my body since the scaffolding. I eat half the slice before I notice I am eating, and Salai is watching me, and Salai’s mouth has done the small private movement that means he has registered my hands trembling.

He says nothing about the trembling.

“You went without me.”

“I did.”

“You could have taken me. It is not a complicated journey.”

“You hate Vinci. The last time I took you, you spent three days asking me when the Florentines were going to learn how to make a proper sausage.”

“It is a fair question. The Florentines hide too much fennel in everything. The fennel does not help.”

“You ate four of them anyway.”

“I was a guest. A guest does not refuse fennel sausage on principle.” He sips from the cup, which is now his cup. “Did Ser Piero ask after me.”

“No.”

“He did not even ask if I was still alive.”

“He would not assume so.”

“That hurts.” He selects an olive, holds it between thumb and forefinger, inspects it for whatever olives are inspected for. “Maestro. Marco came by yesterday.”

I look up.

“He came by the workshop?”

“Twice. The second time he had been drinking. He said the refectory has gone cold, and he is not going back.”

“He is supposed to be back tomorrow.”

“Marco is not going back, Maestro. Marco has, in his own words, decided to be a bricklayer.”

“He is fourteen.”

“He is fourteen and frightened. He says you have started painting Christ in a refectory that is no longer warm, and that the brushes do not behave for you, and that something in the wall watches him from the place where you are not painting the Judas.” Salai pulls another olive from the bowl, examines it, sets it back unchewed. “He used the word watches, Maestro. Three times.”

I do not answer.

“So.” Salai’s eyes settle on the box. “Either Marco has invented a story, which would be the only invention of his career, or you have not been telling me something. Open the box.”

I open the box.

I open it because Salai is watching me, and I have spent twenty-three years in this city building a reputation for not being a man who can be watched into doing things he does not wish to do, and watched is exactly what he is doing. The brass hook lifts. The latch releases. The lid rises on a small hinge I do not remember my grandfather buying.

The smell that comes out of the box is faint, mineral, with a thin thread of something I will think about later and not be able to name. Not incense. Not myrrh. Older than either.

Top layer: a small leather-bound journal, oil-stained at the corners. A loose page folded on top, addressed in my grandfather’s hand.

Middle layer: seven small clay pots, each no larger than a hazelnut shell. Each sealed with red wax, each stamped with a different mark scratched into the seal by a knife-point. Blue ink. Red ink. Gold leaf pressed into the wax. White. Black. Green. And one unmarked.

Bottom layer: a wrapped panel. Linen, tied with cord, the cord knotted in a particular way.

I lift the blue pot first. Hold it up to the brazier. The flame in the brazier should reflect off the wax seal as orange, the way flame reflects off any wax in any room. The flame does not reflect off this wax. The brazier’s light goes into the pot and does not come back. A small dark spot now sits between my hand and the brazier, and the corner of the room behind it has become slightly easier to see.

“That is wrong,” Salai says, with the certainty of a man stating that gravity is operating today as expected.

“Yes.”

I set the blue pot down.

The red is second. The weight is wrong. The pot is the size of a hazelnut shell, should weigh perhaps three drachms; instead it weighs in my hand as if it weighed half a pound. Not from mass. From pull. The pot wants to be set down on the earth, and my fingers tire holding it up against the pull.

I set the red pot down.

The gold pot is cold. Not cool. Cold. Cold enough that when Salai reaches across and touches it with the back of his knuckle, condensation forms in the spaces between his fingers and the wax in three small beads.

“Maestro.” He says it very quietly. “That pot is cold.”

“I know.”

“What is in it?”

“I do not know yet.”

He pulls his hand back from the gold, examines the knuckle, finds nothing wrong with it. He waits for me to lift another pot. I look at the white pot, the black, the green, the unmarked one. I have the sense, from looking at them in the wood of the box, that I do not want to lift them. My grandfather laid them in this order on purpose. The three I have lifted are the three he wanted me to lift first. The four I have not lifted are the four he wanted me not to lift at all.

I close the lid on the middle layer. I lift the loose page from the top of the journal. I read.

I do not read the page aloud. Not yet. I read it once, to myself, and fold it and place it on the bench beside the journal. Salai watches me fold it. He does not ask what it says. He has learned the particular silence that means I will not be asked.

“There is one more thing in the box.”

“I saw.”

I reach into the bottom layer and lift the wrapped panel.

The panel is the size of a man’s face. Approximately ten inches by twelve. The dimensions are exact. I have measured the Judas-space with my eye every day for the last seven months, and I know its proportions. The panel in my hands is the Judas-space.

Coincidences of this kind are not coincidences.

The cord is tied in a knot I last saw my grandfather tie when I was six years old. He taught me to tie it once, in the kitchen of his small farmhouse: the country knot used by men who tie game to a pole and carry it home from the hill. He tied it that day around a rabbit he had killed and given to me for my saint’s day. I remember the cord’s bite into the rabbit’s fur. I remember thinking the knot was kind, because it did not slip even when the rabbit was carried by a child too small to be careful.

I untie the knot.

The dust pattern on the cord is intact until my fingers touch it. No one has handled this cord since my grandfather laid it in the box. For a moment I have the unhelpful sensation of his hands on the cord beneath mine; I let it pass.

The linen falls away. I turn the panel over.

Four old lines of dulled gold frame the face, cracked at the corners. The gold has the patina of decades. Antonio laid it in his thirty-third year, and it has been holding what it was laid to hold ever since, until now.

The face is wrong.

Not crudely wrong. Not amateurishly wrong. The features have been placed correctly by every drawing-master’s rule: the eyes sit in the right plane, the nose has the correct length, the mouth is the right width below the nose. The technique of the underpainting is my grandfather’s, and I recognise the order of his shadow tones, the way he prepares a flesh ground with a green-brown beneath that gives the skin its life.

But the features have been assembled wrong. Not against the rules. Through the rules. The eyes sit slightly too low for the way I have seen Antonio draw a face; the mouth has been pulled, not into an expression, but into the negative space that lives between expressions; the brows are correct, but they have been laid above a forehead that has been drawn the way the wax of a candle has been drawn, halfway to softening. The face is what I would see if I stopped a man’s face halfway through a yawn and froze it where it lost meaning.

This is what the seventeen Judases would have looked like, if any of them had dried.

Salai goes still.

Salai is rarely still. The stillness of Salai is the stillness of a cat that has heard the door of a cage close. He does not approach the panel. He does not come closer than the bench will permit him.

“Whose face was that,” he says.

“Hers. Or what her face becomes when a keeper has set her in a prison and the prison has begun to crack.”

“It looks wrong.”

“It is correct. That is what an imprisoned face looks like. Antonio painted it in his thirty-third year. It held for thirty years. It is failing now.”

“Why is it failing.”

“Because she has found another door. The wall in my refectory.”

Salai is quiet. He looks at the panel again. He sees what I see: the face is not a man’s face, and it never was, although for two days I had let myself think so. The face is hers, half-rendered, half-undone, the door-state of a thing that should have been held closed.

“Turn that one to the wall, Maestro. Now.”

I turn the panel to the wall. I rest it against the leg of the workbench. The half-painted face is now staring at the wood; I cannot see it, the bench can.

“Better,” Salai says. He sits down. His hands lie flat on the bench. He does not pick up an olive. “Read me the letter.”

I read aloud now.

I read aloud because the only way I can stand to read this slowly enough to understand it is to make my mouth do the work my eyes are no longer trustworthy for. Salai sits across the bench, arms folded against his chest the way men stand at funerals when they have decided the priest is taking too long.

My grandfather’s hand is small and meticulous in the early entries; it loosens as the journal goes on. The pages I read from are toward the end.

“There are seven pigments. Three are safe to use. Blue, red, gold. The other four are emergency colours. Do not break their seals unless the alternative is your death or the death of the world.”

Salai’s olive pit clicks against the rim of the bowl.

“The pigments are made from minerals taken from places where she has touched the earth. Each colour retains a fraction of her property. The blue holds depth. The red holds life. The gold holds voice.”

I turn the page.

“I have called her La Famelica, because hunger is the only name she has ever answered to. She has older names. I will not write them. To write them is to invite a visit.”

“Famelica,” Salai says, tasting the word. “The hungry one.”

“Yes.”

“It fits.”

“What is the white.” Salai’s voice. “And the black. And the green.”

“He does not say.”

“He does not say because they should not be said?”

“He does not say because he was tired.”

I keep reading.

“The portrait in the box is the prison I made for her in my thirty-third year. It held for thirty years. I think it is now cracking. I do not know how long it will hold. I do not know whether the wall at Santa Maria delle Grazie is the same prison opening from a different side, or whether she has opened a second door. If you are reading this and the wall is bleeding her through, then it is the same prison, and the second door must be sealed at the same moment as the first.”

I stop. Salai is looking at the wrapped panel against the leg of the workbench. I keep reading.

“The pigments take their price from the painter’s life-record. Memory. Sight. The body’s quiet usefulnesses. The things you do not know you have until you no longer have them. I have spoken twice in my life with pigments, and I have paid each time. I will not tell you what I paid. You will know when you reach for it and it is no longer there.”

The room is quiet. Salai has not moved.

The last entry is dated less than a month ago. The handwriting has lost most of its precision; it is the hand of a man writing through stiff fingers.

“Leonardo, my grandson. I had hoped to die before this letter became necessary. I did not. The work is yours now. I am sorry.”

I close the journal.

The brazier has burned lower. Salai’s olive is gone. The bowl is empty; but he has not eaten the others, he has lined them up by size and left them.

“He knew you would inherit it,” Salai says.

“Yes.”

“Did he know I would be here.”

I do not answer. My hand crosses the bench and finds his wrist. I do not look at him; he does not look at me. I hold his wrist for the length of two breaths. I take my hand back. He keeps his where it was, palm against the wood.

“Maestro.”

“Yes.”

“That last entry. The hand of a man writing through stiff fingers.” He picks an olive from the line he has arranged, the second one, the second smallest. “He was your grandfather. He was eighty-two years old when he wrote that. He was sorry.”

“He was.”

“Then I am sorry for him also.” He pulls the pit out, sets it on the rim. “Read me the rest. The part you skipped.”

I look at him.

“Maestro. You skipped a page. You always skip the page that matters.”

I read the page I had skipped.

The page contains seven names. Seven cities. Seven dates. None of the dates is in this century. The latest is 1304. The names are keepers. The dates are when each keeper died. Failed, the journal says, in Antonio’s hand, beside each name.

The seven failures are men who tried, before my grandfather, to do what my grandfather did at thirty-three: paint her in. Each of them, like the panel now turned to the wall against the workbench leg, failed.

The seventh name is the name of a Florentine. The seventh date is 1304.

Salai counts on his fingers as I read. He uses both hands. He arrives at the answer.

“Eight,” he says. “There are at least eight of you. There were.”

“There were.”

“And now.”

“Now there is one.”

“Tell me about the wall.”

I tell him. I do not tell him cleanly; the wall is not the kind of thing one tells cleanly. I tell him about Marco. I tell him about the seventeen attempts. I tell him about the bell of the falling palette knife. I tell him about her voice in the plaster, her hand on the other side of the plaster, the bulge that was fingers, the smile that was not a smile. I tell him I went to Vinci because I did not know what else to do. I tell him I have come back with my grandfather’s box and a wrapped panel I do not know how to use.

I tell him all of this in perhaps four minutes.

Salai listens. He has retrieved the olives. He picks another from the bowl, slowly, with the particular care a man takes when his hands wish to busy themselves. The pit goes on the rim of the bowl in the place its size would warrant.

“The panel,” he says, “is the same shape as the wall.”

“Yes.”

“Your grandfather made the panel to hold her.”

“I believe so.”

“And she is now in the wall, too.”

“Yes.”

He pulls another olive. He works the pit clean with his teeth in the small private motion he has done since he was ten, and sets the pit beside the first.

“Then either she is in two places, Maestro. Or the two places are the same place. With two doors.”

I stop moving.

Salai notices. He does not look at me. He pulls the third olive.

“If the door is in the wall,” he says, around the olive, “then she has hands on both sides. Close one side, you have closed nothing. She just comes through the other.”

He swallows. He sets the third pit on the rim. The three pits sit in a careful descending row. He has still not looked at me.

He is right.

I do not say it. The thought sits in the room between us. He does not need me to say it; I can see in the line of his shoulders that he knows what he has just said, and that he is pretending not to know, because if he has known it then I have known it, and if I have known it then I have known what we will have to do.

“Salai.”

“Maestro.”

“The panel in your hand.”

He looks down at his hand. There is no panel in it. There is an olive, the fourth one. He has been holding it for some time.

“I have an olive, Maestro. I had three. The first one was very good. The second was acceptable. The third tasted of brine that has been brine for too long, but I ate it out of solidarity with the first two.”

“Salai. Be serious.”

“I am being serious, Maestro. I have just told you the price of an olive. Now you will tell me the price of the other thing.”

“I do not know yet.”

“You do not know yet, or you have been afraid to open it.”

I look at him. He looks at me. The lamp on the bench gutters; the lamp catches his eye and his eye catches the lamp; and for a moment the boy I am looking at is not seventeen, is not the boy who climbed the stairs at ten and refused to leave. He is a man of perhaps thirty, perhaps forty, with my grandfather’s face. Antonio is looking at me through the lamp, the way Antonio looked at me when I was nine and had been caught.

It is a trick of the lamp. The lamp steadies. The boy is seventeen again.

“Salai. You should not be here.”

“Maestro. Where else would I be.”

We prepare the workshop for sleep.

The work is small and practiced. Salai banks the brazier. I set out the two pallets. Salai takes the one nearer the door, the warmer one, because he sleeps cold and I sleep through anything. The pallets are thin. The straw smells of camphor I put in last summer to keep mice out, the camphor has gone faint, and a mouse has investigated. There is a small bitten place at the corner of Salai’s pallet. He notices, and moves the pallet half a foot toward the bench, away from the bitten corner, with the particular concentration he applies to things he wants no one to know he cares about.

He lies down. He is asleep within a minute.

Salai sleeps the way cats sleep: completely, unguarded, his mouth open just enough to show the chip on his upper left tooth he got from biting a melon stone at six, his curls fallen across his forehead. The breath that comes out of him is slow and unconcerned, and I want to draw him, and I cannot draw him because I have set out the candle but I have not the wit to lift a pen.

I lie on my own pallet. I watch the room.

The brazier light is dying. The lamp Salai lit when he came in is the last working light. As the brazier ebbs, the shadows on the wall above the wrapped panel begin to gather. Not a face. Not yet. The outline of where a face might assemble itself.

I do not get up. I do not move. I watch the shadow.

The shadow does not become a face. It remains an outline: the forehead’s edge against the wall, the hollow of the cheekbone, the jaw line, unsettled. A shape that is almost a face. A shape waiting.

The outline is not a face, I think. The outline is what a face would be, if it had time.

The brazier dies entirely. The shadow goes with it. The lamp Salai lit gutters in the last of its oil and goes out without ceremony.

The room is dark. Salai’s breath continues.

In Vinci, when I was nine, my grandfather Antonio put me to bed in the small upstairs room of his farmhouse and stood at the door watching the lamp. He stood there for an hour. I asked him eventually what he was watching. He said: the light, Leonardo, only the light. Sleep. I slept. I dreamed of nothing. In the morning he was not at the door. I assumed he had gone to feed the chickens.

He had not, perhaps, been watching the light.

I dream tonight of my mother’s house in Vinci. There is a child’s hand on a door that should not open. The child is not me. The hand opens the door. The door opens onto a room I cannot describe because rooms in dreams do not stay still long enough to be described.

I wake once before dawn. The room is dark. Salai is still asleep. The shadow is nothing. The wrapped panel against the bench leg is a wrapped panel against a bench leg.

I lie awake until first grey.

Salai wakes first. He has always woken first, even in winters when I have wanted him to sleep through. He sits up, runs a hand through his curls without untangling them, considers the day, and rises.

He crosses to the cabinet for his work-smock. He pulls the smock on over his shirt. He pauses. He looks down at it. He frowns. He shrugs his shoulders, twice. The smock does not give.

“Maestro,” he says. “Do you have a larger one? This is no longer mine.”

I lift my head from the pallet.

Salai is standing in the morning light. The light from the high window is pale and Lombard-grey. His curls catch it the way his curls have caught it since he was thirteen. The smock is taut across his shoulders, the seam showing strain at the back. He has grown. He has been growing for two years; I have been gone, or distracted, or working; and his shoulders are no longer the shoulders of the boy I dressed in this smock the autumn before last.

I have not painted him recently.

The child I fed for seven years is becoming a man. I have not yet looked at him long enough to see who that man is.

“In the cabinet,” I say. “Bottom shelf. The grey one.”

He turns. He goes to the cabinet. He comes back wearing one of my older smocks, too long in the body and too wide in the chest. He does not look ridiculous. He looks like an artist.

He looks like an artist who is becoming a man.

The two are not the same. I have known this longer than I have wanted to.

He comes to the bench. The wrapped panel is still against the leg, face to the wood. The box is closed. The journal is on the bench. The seven pots are arranged on the cloth he laid out last night before sleep.

“Maestro.”

“Yes.”

“Did you sleep?”

“Briefly.”

“Did you decide anything in the night.”

“I decided we test the pigments today.”

He does not flinch. He does not ask which ones, in what order, or whether he is to be in the room when I do it. He picks up the blue pot, the one whose wax devours the light, and holds it for a moment in the morning grey. The corner of his thumbnail is already stained the way an apprentice’s thumbnail is always stained: ground walnut, lead-tin, the particular brown of the inside of an oyster.

He sets the blue pot back down on the cloth.

“All right,” he says. He tilts his head a little to the left, the way he does when he is choosing his words. “I will say this once, Maestro. Twice if you make me. Then we will not have to say it again. Today you may stand at the bench, and I may stand at the doorway, if that is the arrangement you require. I will stand at the doorway. I will not enjoy it. If at any point you decide to die in front of me, that is your business; you have spent years preparing for it, in your own way. But I am not going back to Florence, and I am not going back to Oreno, and I am not going down the stairs of this workshop until what is in your refectory is no longer in your refectory. Yes?”

I look at him.

He looks at me. He is not crying. He is, perhaps, daring himself not to cry.

He says one word.

“We.”

III. THE TESTING

“There are three pigments you may use. There are four you may not. The difference between the two lists is what the using costs.”

Antonio da Vinci, keeper’s journal

Leonardo da Vinci

Leonardo’s workshop, Corte Vecchia, Milan

Late February 1497

Morning is grey. The window above the workbench shows the cold colour I knew from the road back from Vinci, not the silver-grey of Florence but the wet-stone grey of Lombardy in late winter. Salai has lit the brazier and put water on for the muller.

“Salai.”

“Maestro.”

“You will stand at the doorway. Not closer.”

He stops mid-motion. The water for the muller becomes a small lake of refusal in the bowl he is holding.

“Maestro. No.”

“Salai. Listen. If something happens to me, you must be able to leave. You must be at the doorway, where you can leave. Promise me.”

“I am not promising.”

“Then I will not test.”

“You will. You will test in an hour, or you will test in two; you will test today either way, because today is the only day you have.” He sets the bowl down. He does not promise. He walks across the workshop, slowly, until he is at the doorway, and stands there with one shoulder against the frame, his weight on his right foot, his hands doing nothing.

His hands are twitching to come closer.

“I am at the doorway.”

“Thank you.”

I grind the blue. I have ground pigments my entire adult life; the muller on the porphyry stone has a sound I know the way a bricklayer knows the sound of his trowel. The pigment yields under the muller. The pigment becomes finer. The pigment incorporates the oil. The pigment behaves as pigment behaves.

This pigment grinds wrong.

It does not resist. It also does not yield. The texture under the muller has the consistency of something being ground by my hand but not for my hand, as though the grinding is being done with my muscles by another mind, as though I am a tool being borrowed for the moment of its use.

The colour develops on the stone. Blue. Blue like blue should be. Blue like azzurro della Magna never has been. Blue with depth.

I prepare a small panel. Four inches by four. Common pine, primed with gesso. I dip a small brush. I paint a square.

The square is a window into the wood.

Not through. Into. I can see the grain of the wood, the lay of its fibres, at a depth the panel does not have. The panel is half an inch thick. The depth in the painted square does not stop where the panel stops. There is wood below the wood.

Cold air rises from the square against my hand. I cover it with a cloth, the one Salai folded last night and laid out on the bench beside the pots, because Salai had decided last night that today there would be cloths laid out, and that he would lay them.

I look at my fingers. Two of them have the blue on them, the thumb and the index. I cross to the basin and pour the hot water. I rub the stain. The stain does not lift. I try linseed. The stain does not lift. I try the harshest soap I have, the one I use to clean varnish off brushes, and the blue remains under my skin, beneath the surface, a property of who I am now and not a thing on me.

“Maestro.”

“It will not wash off.”

“I can see that.”

This is how walls are made, I think; and I do not say it aloud, because Salai is at the doorway, and he is not promising anything, and he is also not leaving.

We eat. Salai has come back from the canal markets while I was washing my fingers, bringing yesterday’s bread, fresh oil, a hard cheese, and two small fish wrapped in vine leaves he found somewhere. The fish are too small for sale; the market would have thrown them back.

“They were going to feed them to a cat,” he says. “I asked which cat. The fishmonger could not produce one. I said the fish were mine by right of confusion.” He drizzles oil on the bread. “The fishmonger said I was a small Florentine demon. I told him I was a small Milanese demon, the Florentines being known throughout Lombardy for their incompetence at demonry. He laughed. Then he gave me the fish.”

The fish are good. The oil is good. The bread, having sat overnight, has settled into the kind of slightly hard slice that has more flavour than fresh bread does. We eat for some time without speaking.

“Did the blue hurt.”

“No.”

“Did the blue look back.”

“…No.”

“Then either it has not noticed you yet, or it has noticed you and is being patient. Which one.”

I do not answer.

“Maestro. Which one.”

“I do not know.”

Salai cuts the fish with the small knife he has used to cut all of our food since he was twelve. The knife is too small for the fish. He cuts it carefully anyway.

“Good. Then we test the red. Both of us.”

“Salai.”

“You said three pigments. You will not finish three pigments alone. We have three days, perhaps, before whatever is in your refectory finds another way through the plaster, and you cannot do this alone. You are not to test red without me in the room. You are not to test gold without me in the room. We are doing this. You may decide which of us holds the panel and which of us holds the brush. You may not decide whether I am in the room.”

He does not raise his voice. He does not flinch when he says gold. His knife continues the work it has been doing since he was twelve.

“Salai. Listen.”

“I am listening.”

“The man in the box. The one whose face is turned to the wall.”

“Yes.”

“He had an apprentice. The journal does not say what happened to him.”

Salai chews. He swallows. He picks an olive from the bowl, the olives that have come back from yesterday with fresh oil over the old, and pulls the pit.

“Then we will find out, you and I. Yes?”

“Yes.”

He eats. I eat. We finish the fish and the bread and most of the oil. He pushes the dishes aside.

“After.”

“After what.”

“After the red.”

I grind the red.

The red grinds differently than the blue. The blue ground wrong because it did not yield. The red grinds wrong because it yields too eagerly. The pigment turns to paste in three strokes of the muller. The colour develops faster than red develops. The red wants to be ground. The red wants to be ready.

I do not like that the red wants anything.

“Maestro.”

Salai is at the bench. He has carried in a small panel of seasoned pine, primed yesterday by his own hand. He holds the panel at the corners. He has a clean cloth folded over his arm in case there is spill.

“You said the doorway.”

“I changed my mind.”

“You changed your mind.”

“One drop. You hold the panel. I apply.”

“One drop.”

I prepare the brush, the smallest I have for tempera detail work, with a tip of perhaps four hairs. I dip. I lift one drop of red.

The drop hangs from the brush. It is too dark to be red. It is the colour of the inside of a wound an hour after the cut.

I touch the brush to the panel.

The drop transfers. The panel weeps.

Not in the way paint weeps when applied to imperfectly sized wood. Not by capillary action. The drop spreads with a small visible motion of its own, the way ink spreads on paper but slower, and aimed. It carves a slit in the wood. A small slit, perhaps half an inch long, in the place where the drop had been. The slit is wet.

The slit speaks.

The voice is not the voice from the refectory wall. The voice from the refectory wall has been a critic, articulate, a connoisseur of composition. This voice is a woman’s: older, tired, the voice of a woman who has worked hard and loved a child and is calling that child from across a kitchen and a distance.

Salaino.

Salai’s eyes go to the panel.

Salaino. Little dirty one. Little devil. The name his mother gave him. The name he answers to in the workshop. The name she would have called him from the kitchen of the small house outside Oreno where she worked as a servant.

The voice says one more word.

Caterina.

The name is his mother’s name. The name is also my mother’s name. The doubling does not register on his face; it registers on the inside of my chest, which is the cleverness of the voice, which has chosen the one syllable that catches both of us.

Salai drops the panel.

The panel hits the bench with the sound of any board hitting any bench. The red continues to spread. The slit lengthens. The wood begins to flex along the grain the way a small fish flexes when you set it down on a counter. The board is breathing.

“Maestro.”

Salai has stepped back. He has stepped back, but he has not turned around. He has not run. He is, perhaps, daring himself not to run the way last night at the bench he dared himself not to cry.

“Salai.”

I have the palette knife already. I do not remember picking it up. I scrape. I scrape hard. The red comes up reluctantly, in long thin curls. The wood beneath is wet, soft, the colour of something that has been a tree perhaps two days ago. I scrape until I see clean wood. I scrape past clean wood.

I notice, scraping, that my hand is bleeding.

I notice this the way one notices a missing word at the end of a half-remembered sentence. The hand is wet. The wet is not red pigment. The wet is brighter than the red pigment. The palette knife has cut my palm somewhere in the scraping, and I have not felt the cut, and the red on the panel has pulled my blood toward it across the grain, and the red is drinking.

My throat has stopped working.

Salai is staring at the panel; he does not see my hand. The blood is on the underside of the panel where he cannot see. I find words eventually. They come out clipped, as if from a body that is breathing in narrow.

“The blue. Quickly. Cover this.”

Salai moves. He has the blue pot in his hands before I finish the sentence. He scrapes blue onto a brush, the larger brush, the coarse one we use for ground coats. He paints. He paints over the red, over the slit, over the bleeding wood. The blue settles over the red the way water settles over a fire that has begun to die.

The blue does what the blue is for.

The voice goes silent. The wood stops breathing. The slit closes under the blue, sealed not by physical adhesion but by something I will not be able to describe to anyone who has not used the blue. The blue makes a wall. I felt it as it happened; the blue made a wall between the surface of the wood and what was on the other side of the wood, and what was on the other side of the wood was the same thing that was on the other side of the plaster at Santa Maria delle Grazie.

Salai turns to me. He sees my hand. His face does what his face does when he is afraid and refusing to show me he is afraid.

“Maestro.”

“It will close.”

“It will not close.”

He has the cloth he had folded over his arm. He wraps my hand without asking. He works fast. He ties the cloth tight; he does not meet my eyes.

“Maestro.”

“Yes.”

“She used her name. My mother’s name.”

“And mine.”

He stops. He has not heard that. He has not, for the four seconds it takes him to comprehend it, known that his mother and mine share a name. He looks at me. He looks at the panel. He looks back at me.

“Both our mothers.”

“Yes.”

“She is using both of them.”

“Yes.”

Salai sits down on the floor of the workshop, against the leg of the workbench, on the side opposite the wrapped panel. He sits down hard. He does not cry. He does what he did last night when I had decided we would test the pigments today: he begins, after a moment, to laugh.

It is a small laugh. It is not amused.

“Maestro. We are in trouble.”

“Yes.”

The red is for life. And life knows what it is hungry for.

Late afternoon. The bandage on my hand is heavier than it was; Salai has changed it twice. The cut continues to weep small amounts of slow blood, dark and ordinary.

We do not test red again. We do not need to. The board the red opened is now under two coats of blue, leaning against the back wall of the workshop, where it can see no one and no one can see it. Salai has not looked at it in two hours.

He brings me a fragment of plaster from the small pile by the door, the pieces that fell when the carpenter built the new shelves last summer, plaster Salai has been meaning to clear away for six months. The fragment is the size of a child’s palm.

I open the gold pot.

The pot is colder than it should be. It is colder than the cold pot was this morning. There is frost on the seal, frost that did not exist when I opened the box last night, frost that has formed during a day in a heated workshop. The frost is white against the red wax.

Salai stands back. He has learned, today, when to stand back.

I break the seal. The pot is not gold; the gold is. The pot is a small clay vessel containing what looks at first like ground gilt and reveals itself, when I tilt it toward the lamp, as a powder finer than any gilt I have ever ground, with light coming off it the way light comes off a mirror tilted just so. The light is not the lamp’s. The light is the gold’s own.

I scrape a small amount of gold onto a brush. I paint a single line on the plaster fragment. One line. One stroke. Perhaps two inches long. The gold lies on the plaster as gold lies on plaster, except for the small private fact that the gold is glowing.

I say one word.

“Leonardo.”

The plaster says it back.

The voice is my own voice. Exactly my own voice. The pitch. The slight rasp from too little sleep. The particular way the o sounds in my mouth, which is a Florentine o and not a Milanese o. The plaster has just spoken my name in my voice.

The plaster says it again.

“Leonardo. Soon.”

I did not say soon.

Salai’s hand goes to the chisel on the bench. He has been waiting, perhaps, for the moment when the chisel will be needed. He brings it down on the plaster fragment. He brings it down again. He brings it down a third time. The plaster is dust on the floor.

He stands looking at the dust.

“Maestro,” he says, without lifting his eyes. “Did you hear.”

“Yes.”

“The second word. Was that yours.”

“No.”

“Yours is now. You always say now. You have never said soon in your life.”

“I know.”

“Then whose was that.”

“Mine.”

He looks at me.

“Mine,” I say, “in the way the panel was your mother’s voice and not your mother. It used my mouth. It practised the o.”

We sweep the dust into the brazier. The dust burns blue, not orange. Not the colour ordinary plaster dust burns. The dust burns the colour of the blue pigment I painted onto the slit this morning, the colour of the wall the blue makes.

I seal the gold pot. The frost on the seal has not gone, even after the pot has stood open in a heated room. Salai watches me seal it. He watches the brazier where the blue dust is still burning faintly along one log.

He does not say what he is thinking. I know what he is thinking. He is thinking that the gold takes what is given to it and gives it back, and is therefore the colour of binding. We have learned this without being told.

Night.

Salai has been asleep for an hour. The brazier is banked. The bandage on my hand has soaked through to a soft brown, and for some time now I have been meaning to lift my head from the pallet and change it.

I have not lifted my head.

I am in a gallery.

I was not in a gallery the moment before. I do not remember closing my eyes. The gallery is vaulted, long, lit by oil lamps in iron sconces. The ceiling has the high arched echo of the refectory at Santa Maria delle Grazie. The walls are stone, and the walls hold paintings.

Paintings on both walls, paintings hung close. Some I recognise: my own Annunciation from when I was twenty, the unfinished Adoration that sits in Florence as a brown ghost. Some I do not. A Crucifixion in the manner of nothing I have seen, by a hand that worked with light the way I work with light, except where I would have laid a glaze the painter has laid a void; the place where Christ’s face should be is, in this Crucifixion, the place where the wall is. Beside it, a portrait of a young woman with a single eye larger than the other, painted as if to be looked at by someone who would not notice that it was wrong. An Annunciation by a different hand, with the angel’s wings spread in a geometry I cannot account for.

The unfamiliar paintings are accomplished. They are the work of people who could paint.

They are the work of keepers.

I walk the length of the gallery. The lamps burn rancid; I smell tallow that has gone past use, the sour smell of a candle burning to the wick. The paintings are hung in chronological order. I know this because I can date the techniques: the earliest is a Byzantine icon, then an early Tuscan Madonna in the manner of Cimabue, then a Sienese altarpiece. Each of them shows the same thing, the same small private wrongness, in a different style. A door painted into a wall that should be solid. A figure rendered in a pose that almost makes sense. A face with a smile no painter would render except by mistake.

Seven paintings. There are seven paintings. I count them as I walk.

Maestro.

She is at the far end of the gallery. She does not approach. I cannot see her clearly; the light at her end is dimmer.

Your Christ’s left hand.

I turn. My own Cenacolo is on the wall beside me, smaller than its real proportions but recognisable.

You have set it palm-up. Open. Generous. This is wrong. He has just said: one of you will betray me. His hand should be closed. Or, better, pointing. The composition does not bear his openness. You have made him too gentle for the moment.

She is correct.

The apostles. Arranged as a frieze. Look. Three, three, Christ, three, three. You are too symmetrical, Maestro. Real men do not cluster in symmetries. They overlap. They lean. You have made them obedient to the wall behind them.

She is correct again.

And Judas. Judas you have not finished because you do not know what he is. You are too kind to him. You imagine a moneylender. A cruel man. A simple narrative. Judas is not a cruel man. Let me show you what he is.

On the wall beside the unfinished Cenacolo, a new painting appears. A face. The face is of a kind man, a man with the soft eyes of someone who has loved his teacher very much, a man whose betrayal would be the more terrible because of the love.

The face is correct. The face is exactly what Judas should be.

Dimmi: what does it mean that her composition is better than mine?

Yes, she says, as if the dream has read me too. I can teach you composition, Maestro. I can show you how to make the apostles cluster. I can finish your bronze horse, the one that will be melted in two years for cannon by men who do not know what bronze is for. I can give you Judas. Together, you and I, could complete the work of your life.

“What is the price.”

The dream-room is silent for a long moment.

What it has always been, Maestro. The same price your grandfather refused to pay.

I look at the seven paintings. I look back to the far end of the gallery, where she stands or does not stand.

“And what did the other seven pay.”

She does not answer. The dimness at her end of the gallery deepens.

The eighth frame, the one nearest her, is not yet filled. The frame is there. The wall behind the frame is the wall.

Soon, she says, and the word is in my own voice, the way the plaster said it this afternoon. Soon you will hang here. Beside the others. Your face will be the eighth.

I wake. I wake the way a man wakes from drowning. Salai is already at my pallet. His hand is on the back of my neck; his other hand is steadying the wooden bowl he has placed in front of me. I empty my stomach into the bowl. The bowl smells of bile and the wine from dinner. I am shaking. I have been shaking since the scaffolding.

“Maestro.”

“I am here.”

“Was she.”

“Yes.”

“What did she say.”

I look at Salai. His face is very young and very awake in the brazier light. The line of his jaw is the line of the boy who climbed those stairs at ten. The line is changing. I have not stopped to watch it change.

“She knows my work better than I do. And she is collecting us.”

Dawn comes slowly. We have not slept since the dream. We sit at the workbench. The wrapped panel is between us, still wrapped, still tied with my grandfather’s country knot, which I retied last night because there was nothing else to do with my hands.

Salai works it out.

“We need to seal both prisons at once.”

“Yes.”

“Tell me the geometry.”

“You and I, both of us at once. I paint Judas. You paint the portrait.”

“You have been failing at Judas for seven months.”

“Yes. And tonight I will not fail at Judas. Because tonight Judas will not be looking out.”

“Eyes inward.”

“Toward Peter’s knife. The gaze that would open the door is held inside the painting. The door cannot open while the gaze is held.”

He nods slowly.

“And the portrait.”

“You paint the portrait. The small one. The wrapped one. At the same moment. Same gesture. We bind both prisons in the same act.”

“With the gold.”

“With the gold. Last. Both panels.”

“This will cost us.”

“Yes.”

“Tonight.”

“Tonight.”

He puts both his palms flat on the bench in front of him and looks at his own hands. His hands have not yet been stained. He notices this. He looks at my two blue fingertips. He looks at the bandage on my palm. He looks at his own clean hands, the hands of a seventeen-year-old who has not yet paid anything.

“Maestro.”

“Yes.”

“When I paint the portrait. With the gold. Will I be the one paying.”

He has worked it out himself. He should not be able to. He is not a keeper. He should not be able.

“Yes. Both of us. Each paying what the work demands of the painter.”

“Good.”

“Salai.”

“It is good, Maestro. I would rather pay than be unable to help you.”

He looks at me then.

“I have not been a good apprentice.”

“Salai.”

“I have stolen from you, lied to you, and traded your second-best brushes for wine on three documented occasions, possibly more. I have been il Salaino. I have been the little devil. Today I am going to be the man who paints the portrait. Will you let me be the man who paints the portrait.”

I do not say yes. He does not need me to.

We will not sleep before the ritual. We lie down anyway.

The body needs rest. The mind refuses. The mind is composing every gesture of what we are about to do, every stroke, every brush, every order in which the pots will be opened and closed. The mind is also, separately, composing my mother’s face. I have been looking at her face in memory since the dream, the way one looks at something to confirm it is still there. The face is still there. I do not know if it will be there tomorrow.

Leonardo on his pallet. Salai on his. The brazier between us, low. The bandage on my hand is wet. I changed it three hours ago; it is wet again. The cut has decided what it is going to be. It is going to be a thing that remembers.

Salai reaches across the gap between the pallets. His hand finds mine. The bandage is damp under his fingers. He does not say anything about the damp. He does not let go.

“Maestro.”

“Yes.”

“If your mother and my mother share a name, then we share something I had not yet decided whether to claim.”

“Salai.”

“I claim it.”

“It is not a thing one claims. It is a thing one finds out one is.”

“Then I have found out.”

I do not answer. The brazier hisses. One coal fails. The cold creeps up through the floor toward us, the wet Lombard cold that gets in at the ankles first.

We do not let go. We do not sleep.

The day does not pass. It thickens. The bells mark Prime, then Terce, then Sext, then None, each office arriving from the lower city as if time still believes itself useful. The bells mean nothing to us except that the dark is coming.

The bandage is damp. Salai’s hand is over the bandage. We wait.
