IV. THE PRICE OF DOORS

“The keeper does not save what he protects. The keeper pays for it instead.”

Antonio da Vinci, final entry in the journal

Leonardo da Vinci

Leonardo’s workshop, Corte Vecchia & Refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan

Late February 1497

We leave the workshop at the third hour after sunset.

Salai carries the wrapped panel against his chest, the cord retied in my grandfather’s country knot. I carry the wooden box with the seven pots, the small lamp, two extra brushes, a flask of linseed against the cold, and a stoppered jar of mulled wine I do not intend to drink. The streets of Milan after dark are not the streets they are by daylight. By daylight Milan is a city. By dark Milan is a series of small lit rooms separated by alleys in which one does not walk if one prefers to keep one’s purse.

We walk. Salai goes ahead. He knows these alleys; he has known them since he was eight, in the years before he was an apprentice, when he was a boy on the Naviglio earning a piece of bread by carrying the fishmonger’s basket. The watch-fires of the city guard burn at the corners. The dogs at Sant’Eustorgio bark twice and stop. The cold comes off the canal and into the lungs as a separate weight.

Salai does not speak. I do not speak.

We reach Santa Maria delle Grazie at perhaps the fourth hour. The cloister is empty. The monks are at compline; I can hear their voices, distant, through the connecting wall, the late Office sung by men who do not yet know what is in the refectory three doors away from them.

I take my key from my belt. The lock turns. The iron clicks. We are in.

The refectory is colder than the cloister. The plaster by the Judas-space has the particular cold of plaster that has been waiting for a thing.

Salai sets the wrapped panel on the workbench I had Marco bring in last summer and which Marco has now abandoned. He unties the cord. He folds the linen. He turns the panel face-up.

The face is still wrong. The face still has the half-yawn that lives between expressions, and after two days under linen on my workbench the face has not aged.

“Maestro.”

“Salai.”

“It is looking at us.”

“It has always been looking at us.”

He does not flinch this time. He has been preparing himself for this for two days and a night. He lifts the small bench-lamp I gave him to carry and sets it so that the panel is lit from the same angle as the wall above us, the same light, the same shadow plane. He has thought about this. He has thought about it without telling me.

He removes his coat. Beneath it he is wearing the grey smock from yesterday morning, the one too long in the body and too wide in the chest, the one that makes him look like an artist becoming a man.

He picks up a brush. He looks across the refectory at me. The look is the one I used to give my master Verrocchio when I was sixteen, on the day he handed me the unfinished angel in the Baptism of Christ and said: finish it. I have other work.

I nod.

We begin.

The refectory is a long room, vaulted, with the long table running its length and the great Christ on the wall at the head. The scaffolding I have been working from for two years stands against the wall to the right of the table. Salai’s bench is set against the left wall, where the light from the bench-lamp can reach the small panel without compromising my own.

We have set up the room so that he is in my peripheral vision and I am in his.

I climb the scaffolding. Each rung feels longer tonight. By the third rung my left knee tells me what my body has been telling me since the road back from Vinci, that it knows what is coming, and that it does not approve. By the fifth rung I am at the level of the apostles’ shoulders, and I can see Salai below me, at the bench, the small lamp lit, the panel face-up on a folded cloth.

The Judas-space waits.

I have not looked at the Judas-space at this hour, in this light, before tonight. The space is darker than the surrounding plaster, by which I mean: the surrounding plaster reflects the lamp, and the Judas-space does not.

Maestro.

Her voice. In the wall. Through the wall. From the panel below. She is in both. She is in the room.

You are about to ruin my evening.

It is a joke. Her voice is making a joke. The voice I heard a week ago could not have made a joke. The voice has been practising. The voice has been getting closer.

Let us bargain.

I do not answer. I prepare my brushes. I have brought four: the smallest, for the irises of the eyes; the middle, for the contours; the larger, for the broad fill of cheek and neck; and a fourth, a flat, for gold.

Maestro. I will not be subtle. Listen.

I dip the first brush in the underpainting, the red ochre I have ground from regular pigment, the safe pigment from the cabinet of my Milan studio, not from my grandfather’s box. I will not use the seven pots on the underpainting. I will use them only at the moment of the eyes, the moment of the mouth, the moment of the sealing.

To you, Maestro. I offer your bronze horse. I offer the Adoration. I offer the diving apparatus, the flying machine, the mechanical lion, the city of Imola redrawn on perfect maps. I offer everything you have begun and not finished. I will finish them in your hand. You will be the only painter and engineer in history whose work was completed.

I lay the underpainting on Judas’s cheek. The ochre takes. The brush behaves.

To the boy. Salaino. I offer your mother. The version of her you remember from before she gave you up. The kitchen at Oreno. The smell of bread. The dress with the blue stitching at the wrist. I will give them all back.

Salai’s brush pauses. For a heartbeat. Then he continues. The ochre takes. The brush behaves.

You are not listening, she says.

We do not answer.

The voice changes register. The voice has been the critic and the tempter; now it is the buyer who has decided the merchant is wasting her time.

Then I will tell you the cost of refusing me, and I will speak plainly because you have not earned politeness. Maestro: your Cenacolo will not survive the century. The plaster you have insisted on for this painting is wrong for fresco, and the painting will begin to peel within twenty years. I have known this since you laid the first coat. I have permitted it. I will withdraw my permission tonight, and the painting will not survive fifty.

She is correct about the plaster. I know this. I have known it since I chose it.

And the boy. Salaino. The boy is not yours and never will be. He will leave you for a French king and he will marry and he will die before he is fifty, in a way I would have spared him from. I have seen this. It is on the wall behind me.

I look down. Salai is painting. His brush moves. He has heard her. He is not looking up.

Maestro.

“No.”

Maestro.

“No.”

The voice becomes patient again. The patience now is the patience of a thing settling in for a longer fight.

Very well. Begin. I will be here.

I take up the brush. I begin Judas’s eye.

I paint.

The underpainting goes on the cheekbones, the brow, the hollow under the eye, the soft place beneath the lip. I render Judas as my grandfather rendered faces: green-brown under the flesh, the way Florentine masters laid the ground in the last century. This is not how I would paint Judas in a normal commission. This is how a keeper paints. I learned the technique by reading my grandfather’s journal twice in the last forty hours.

Below me Salai paints.

Salai is rendering Famelica. He has, on the bench beside the lamp, Antonio’s cracked prison-panel; he is not making a copy of it. He is painting over it, completing what my grandfather left half-finished, renewing the binding where the prison has cracked. The same panel. The same prison. New gold to seal what the old gold could no longer hold.

The smell in the room is wrong. The smell of fresh pigment in a room should be linseed and walnut oil with the slight base note of the binder. The smell tonight is the same plus something I do not have a word for, the smell of a place becoming a different place. I have stopped trying to identify the second smell. I am painting through it.

The voice has not yet returned.

Maestro.

There. There is the voice. The voice is closer.

I lift the second brush. I begin the mid-tones of Judas’s flesh. The skin of the face begins to develop on the wall in front of me, in the place where the seventeen Judases failed, and as the face develops I understand for the first time why it failed seventeen times.

Dimmi: why has the face failed seventeen times?

It failed because I was painting a man. The face is not a man; the face is a key, the shape of the lock the door is set in. The face has the proportions of a man because the door needs a man-shaped key to hold it shut. I have been trying to paint a character. The wall has been waiting for a function.

I paint the function.

The face develops on the wall as the seventeenth attempt would have developed if I had let it dry. The face that came through under the wet pigment that afternoon and made me reach for the palette knife, that face, is the face I am now painting on purpose. The same face. The same mouth. The same calm, ordinary, decided expression of a small functionary at his master’s table.

I am painting her Judas.

I understand this as I paint. The terror of understanding it does not stop my hand; my hand has gone past terror into the place beyond terror, the place where the body works because the body has been told to work and no longer asks for permission.

Yes, Maestro, she says, quietly. Yes. This is the face.

“Salai. The portrait.”

“I have her, Maestro. I have her halfway. The mouth is the difficult part.”

“The eyes last. Same moment. Mine and yours.”

“Yes.”

The lamp on the bench sputters. The flame on the scaffolding lamp sputters. Both lamps are burning low. Both will go before midnight.

Salai paints the mouth. The mouth on the portrait is exactly the mouth I have heard since the scaffolding, soft, intelligent, slightly amused. He has heard her too. He has put the amusement on the mouth.

You hear me well, Salaino. You paint me well. You will make a magnificent keeper.

Salai’s brush pauses. Holds.

“Salai. Do not listen.”

“I am not listening, Maestro.”

“You paused.”

“I paused because the mouth required pausing. I am painting her mouth, not the mouth of the voice.”

He is lying. He paused because she said keeper. He paused because he heard, in the word, the weight of his own future. I do not say so. He needs to keep painting. The mouth has to be finished before the eyes.

The mouth is finished. The two faces are now almost complete. Mine on the wall, his on the panel. Both are missing the eyes.

The refectory door bangs open.

Not unlocked. Bangs. The iron handle on the inside of the door clatters once as the outside push catches the latch wrong; the inside latch I locked an hour ago has held against three pulls and now gives on the fourth, the wood splintering at the housing. Bandello has used the spare key with insufficient patience.

He stands in the door.

He is in a white woollen night-robe over a dark tunic, the slippers of a man who has come straight from his cell. He has a lamp. He has also a small leather strap I think is the prior’s discipline-strap and which he has perhaps picked up out of confused instinct. He smells of incense and the bitter herb the Dominicans drink at compline against the cold.

He sees me on the scaffolding. He sees Salai at the bench. He sees the half-painted face on the wall in the lamplight, and he sees the half-painted face on the panel.

“Maestro Leonardo…”

He stops mid-sentence.

His face does the thing a face does when it has just calibrated the situation against what the situation cannot be. It is a small adjustment, the size of a knuckle, but I have watched faces my whole life and I see his face make it.

“What in the name of God…”

“Father, please. Step back. Step back into the cloister.”

It is Salai’s voice. Salai has come off the bench, brush still in his hand. The portrait on the bench is unfinished. Salai is between Bandello and the door, between Bandello and me, between Bandello and the wall. He is also taller than Bandello by half a hand and broader than Bandello by a shoulder, and he is seventeen and the Prior is sixty-two.

“Boy. Get out of my way.”

“Father. With respect. Step back.”

“That is vandalism. He is, what is he…”

The Prior takes a step into the room. Toward the wall.

The Judas-space pulses.

Bandello sees it. Bandello sees what cannot be there. His face does another small calibration. This one is larger.

“Madre di Dio.”

“Father. Outside. Please.”

Salai puts a hand on Bandello’s shoulder. Not violent. Not unkind. The hand of an apprentice asking a master to step away from a kiln. The Prior shakes him off; he comes another step into the room; my hand on the scaffolding has already taken up the next brush, the smallest brush, the brush for the iris of the eye. I dip into the gold pot. I cannot wait. I begin the eye.

I begin the eye, and my hand slips.

It does not slip much. It slips the width of one hair of the brush. The iris of Judas’s eye, which was meant to look inward toward Peter’s knife, has been laid with the pupil a hair’s breadth too far toward the left of the iris. The eye is now looking outward. Toward the viewer.

The room exhales.

She is through.

She is in the room.

Not as a voice. Not as a presence. As a displacement. The air of the refectory becomes the air of somewhere else, and for one second the smell I had no word for has a word, the smell is the smell of a thing that eats the inside of a wall and has waited eighty-three years to eat what is on the outside of one.

Salai screams once.

The Prior screams the longer scream. The Prior is on his knees on the marble of the refectory, the discipline-strap fallen from his hand, and he is reciting the Office of the Dead in a Latin that has lost most of its syntax.

I have no palette knife. I left it at the workshop. I have the brush, and I have my hand.

I scrape the gold from the iris with my fingernail.

The nail splits. The blood comes. The gold lifts. The eye is plaster again, raw, scoured, ready. I redip the brush, and I lay the iris a second time, and this time my hand does not slip, and the pupil sits in the iris as it ought to sit, and the eye of the painted Judas turns inward and looks at Peter’s knife.

The door begins to close.

She makes a sound I will not describe in this journal. She makes the sound an animal makes when the trap closes on the leg it had thought it could pull free.

Salai is at the bench. He has not stopped painting. He has the brush for his portrait. He is laying the iris of her painted eye now, the same moment, the same gesture. He paints. He paints. He paints.

The eye of the portrait opens. The eye looks at us. The eye is hers.

The cost begins.

I do not feel it the way I had imagined I would feel it. I had imagined pain. I had imagined sickness. I had imagined the body’s protest against something taken from it. What I feel instead is quiet. Specific small quiet. The kind of quiet a room takes on when a clock that has been ticking for some time stops ticking.

In my mind, my mother stands in a Tuscan summer-courtyard. She lifts me. She is twenty-three years old. The sun is on the back of her neck. She turns her face toward mine. She is smiling, the small smile she gave me only when no one else was watching, the smile that was for the two of us.

Her face begins to soften.

Not blur. Soften. The way wax softens before melting. The contours of her cheek, the bridge of her nose, the place where her eyes met her brow, the geometry begins to lose its precision. I try, on the scaffolding, with the brush still in my hand, with the gold still wet on Judas’s iris, to hold her face in my mind. I hold for a heartbeat. Two. I hold by sheer will. The image continues to soften.

When I let her go, she has the dimensions of a face but no features.

I will not get her back. I am paying.

On the bench, Salai paints. The portrait’s eye is open now. The other eye is forming. Salai’s hand is steady. His face has done something I do not have a name for. He has stopped blinking. He blinks now twice, in quick succession, as if testing whether blinking still does what blinking should do.

He looks at the lamp. He looks at his brush. He looks at the small jar of blue beside the gold.

“Maestro,” he says, very quietly. “The blue.”

“What about the blue.”

“The blue is not blue.”

“Salai…”

“The blue, Maestro, is grey. The jar is grey. The bench is grey. The flame is the colour of the flame. The wood is the colour of the wood. The blue is grey.”

He is paying. He keeps painting.

The portrait’s second eye opens. Salai paints it without looking down at the panel; he is looking at the wall, at me, at the lamp, at anything that will tell him the colour blue is somewhere else in the room.

I want to climb down. I want to be at his shoulder. I cannot. The work is not done. We have eyes; we do not yet have the sealing gold. The sealing gold must be the last stroke. It has to be the same stroke. Both of us at once.

We carried it to the refectory.

I remember Salai’s hands around the linen at the corners of the panel as we crossed the cloister. I remember him setting the panel on the bench. I remember him untying the cord, folding the linen, lifting the wrapping away.

But the cord is still tied. I see it from the scaffolding. The country knot my grandfather taught me at six is intact on the panel below.

The panel on the bench is the one Salai has been painting all night.

Both are true.

The room has had the panel the whole time. The room is also receiving the panel we carried from the workshop. Memory is the cost. The memory is going. I am inside the going.

I find the brush in my hand. I find the gold. I find Salai’s eyes, across the room, looking up at me.

“Now.”

“Now.”

We paint the seal.

The seal is the gold on the eyelashes. Not the iris. The lashes. The line of fine gold that holds the eye closed when the door wants to open. We have understood this in the last quarter-hour from a journal page neither of us has read; we have understood it because we are keeping, and the keeping is teaching us as we go.

I paint the lashes of Judas’s left eye. Salai paints the lashes of Famelica’s right eye. We move at the same rate. We breathe at the same rate. The two faces, his small one on the bench, mine large on the wall, develop the gold line at the same moment.

The Prior is silent on the marble. He has finished the Office of the Dead. He has begun a Psalm I do not recognise; the words are Latin but the rhythm is his own, the way a frightened man recites when he can no longer remember the verses he was taught and is making the cadence up by feel. He is not looking at us; he is looking at the floor, at the small worn place on the marble where the procession of monks has placed its feet for two hundred years.

I finish Judas’s lashes. Salai finishes Famelica’s.

Then, because the mouth is how she spoke, Salai draws one fine thread of gold along the seam of her painted lips. The line is so thin it is almost not a line. The line is the difference between a mouth that can open and a mouth that cannot. He lifts the brush; the gold sets; the seam holds.

There is one more gesture. Salai sets down the small brush and lifts the flat one, the wider brush we use for ground coats. He dips it in the gold. He lays four lines along the four edges of the small panel: top first, then right, then bottom, then left. Each line is a single unbroken stroke, the way the gilders of Florence paint a frame. The gold sets the boundary. The gold tells the prison where it ends.

He finishes with the lower-left corner.

My wall has its frame already. The architecture of the Cenacolo is its own painted frame; the lunettes, the painted pilasters, the ceiling-coffers I designed at the beginning of this work. Gold along an edge of the wall is not needed. The wall is its own gilt.

The room becomes quiet.

The quiet is not the quiet of an empty room. The quiet is the quiet of a room that has just been entered by no one, the quiet a room has after a door that has been open all winter has finally closed.

Maestro.

Her voice. Different. Diminished. Coming through the gold rather than around it.

Did you notice the eyes?

I look at the wall.

The eyes of my painted Judas are looking inward, toward Peter’s knife. The gaze is held. The door is sealed.

But beneath the gold, in the iris of the left eye, I have left a small mark. A tiny smudge. The hair-breadth slip from earlier, which I scraped with my fingernail, has left a faint discoloration that the gold has covered but not erased. The mark is not visible to anyone who does not know it is there. The mark is visible to her, and to me, and now to Salai, who has come down from the bench and is standing at the foot of the scaffolding looking up.

Did you notice the eyes, Maestro?

“I have noticed.”

The door is closed. But the door is not perfectly closed. A door imperfectly closed is a door that can be opened.

“I know.”

Not tonight. Not next year. But.

“I know.”

We will meet again, Maestro. You. And the boy. And whoever you teach next. We will meet again because the gold has dried over a flaw, and the flaw will be there as long as the gold is there, and the gold will be there as long as your wall stands, and your wall will not stand as long as you have promised the Dominicans it will. I have all the time, Maestro. I have all the time.

The voice fades. The voice does not vanish; the voice fades. The voice is now behind a wall I have spent my entire night building.

I let go of the brush.

The brush falls from the scaffolding. The brush hits the marble. The brush makes the sound a brush makes when a brush hits marble. Not a bell. A brush.

Salai is below me. He is looking up at me. His face is in the lamplight; he has caught the lamplight with his left eye, and his left eye is doing the small thing eyes do when an eye is no longer seeing all the colours an eye used to see.

“Maestro,” he says. “Come down. Please.”

I come down.

We are alive.

We sit on the floor of the refectory, against the wall opposite the Cenacolo. The marble is cold under us; the cold goes through the wool of my smock and the wool of his and finds the wet places on my hand where the blood has not yet stopped. Salai’s left hand is on my left wrist. He has not taken it off in some minutes. I have not asked him to.

The Prior has gone. I did not see him leave. He left some time during the sealing, in a silence I had not heard happen, while I was finishing the lashes. The discipline-strap is still on the floor where he dropped it. The door of the refectory is open; the cold air of the cloister is in the room. I do not know what he will say, or to whom; I know only what I saw on his face when he saw what cannot be there, and a man whose face has done that does not, in my experience, speak of it.

Outside, the bells have begun the Office of Lauds. The monks are awake. They will be in their stalls; they will not come to the refectory until the breakfast hour. We have perhaps two hours before they find us.

The wall is dry.

I have looked at it twice since coming down. The Judas is finished. The Judas’s gaze is held. The composition closes around him in the way I had refused for fourteen months to let it close. He is unmistakable as Judas. He is also unmistakable as the man I would have painted if I had been a better painter and a worse man. The wall, as a painting, will be considered a masterpiece by men who do not know what is sealed beneath the gold of the left eye.

The portrait is on the bench.

The portrait is the face of a woman I have never seen and now will see in dreams for the rest of my life. Her expression is calm, intelligent, slightly amused. Her eyes are the eyes of a thing that has agreed to wait. The portrait will go back to Vinci with me; I will carry it the way my grandfather carried his seven failed predecessors with him, in their failures, in his life-record, until the moment he gave the box to my father with instructions to give it to me.

I will, when I am older, paint another. I do not yet know this. The painting I will paint will not be of her. The painting will be of a woman I have not yet met, though her smile is already finding its way toward me. The painting will, however, be of the same thing. I will not understand this until I am dying. I will understand many things only when I am dying.

“Salai.”

“Maestro.”

“Your eye.”

“My left. The blue is gone. The other colours are mostly. The light is bright on that side. I will manage.”

“Salai. I am sorry.”

He is quiet for a while.

“I am not sorry.”

“Salai…”

“I am not. I had a clean hand last night. Tonight I have a useful hand. The hand that painted her eyes is the hand that will paint everything I paint for the rest of my life. It is a better hand than the hand I had last night.”

He turns his head to look at me. The left eye, the one that has lost the blue, has a fineness to it I have not seen before; it is the eye of a man who knows what he is looking at, because he has paid for what he is looking at.

“Maestro. I remember loving you.”

I do not answer. I cannot. The face of my mother is gone, and I cannot give her face back to him, and there is no word in my body that is large enough for what he has just said. I take his hand.

He says it again, not because he needs to, but because he has decided this is a thing he is going to be able to say.

“I remember loving you.”

We sit on the cold marble.

Outside, the bells continue.

Tomorrow, we will begin pretending nothing happened.

chapters.title: EPILOGUE
chapters.content:
EPILOGUE

“The work is never over. The work is only inherited again.”

Antonio da Vinci, opening of the keeper’s journal

Leonardo da Vinci

A rented workshop, Florence

Spring 1502

The compass refuses to draw a true circle.

I have tried three times this morning. The radius is set. The legs are tight. The Florentine paper under my hand is good Fabriano stock, smooth, ground with bone in the proper old method. The compass-point holds its centre, the drawing-point follows the arc, and the arc drifts.

It drifts by perhaps a hair, perhaps less. The drift is consistent; the drift is the same on each attempt; the drift is small enough that no other man working in this room would notice it. I notice it. Such things were once the simplest measurements my hand could make.

A circle, for me, was once the simplest thing the hand could do. The wrist remembered the radius. The shoulder kept the plane. The mind did not have to participate. The line closed itself.

The line no longer closes itself.

The fourth attempt does not close either. I set the compass down. I pick it up. I set it down again. I look at my left hand. The hand is fifty-one next April. The hand still has the two blue fingertips; the blue has not faded. The bandaged cut across the palm is now a thin red line that has not faded either. The hand is the same hand. The hand has learned that it has been used.

I will learn to draw a circle by other means.

I try once more, this time to please myself, to remember the face of the woman who taught me what a circle was, a young Tuscan farmwife who lifted me at the age of three and said guarda, Leonardo, la luna è il cerchio del cielo. The sun was on the back of her neck. The smile was for the two of us. The smile lived only between her and me, and now it lives in no one, because the face is gone.

I have known the face was gone for some years now. I keep trying to find it. I keep finding the shape where the face was, the way one finds the chair when the lamp is out and there is no lamp.

I set the compass down.

Salai is at the window.

He stands in the morning light with his face turned toward where I am, which is not the same as looking at me. His eyes have, in the last six months, begun to whiten in the way old men’s eyes whiten when the body has finished with light. He has been at the window since first prayer. He can feel the heat of the young spring sun even when he cannot quite see what is in it.

He paints, when he paints, from a low stool with his face perhaps a hand’s-breadth from the panel. He paints what he can paint: drapery, backgrounds, architecture. I paint the faces. We have made it work. We have made many things work that no one looking from outside the room would think could be made to work.

The blue, he says, has not come back. The grey has only deepened. The yellow has begun to dim. He does not complain. He has never complained. He whistles, sometimes, the small Milanese tune his mother sang at Oreno; he whistles it in this Florentine room two hundred miles from her, and he whistles it for me, who has forgotten my own.

Florence in April smells of wet stone and new green and the morning smoke of the laundresses’ fires in the alleys behind the Annunziata.

A boy at our door.

He has a letter.

The letter is from a merchant.

The wax is sealed with a small bird, a song-thrush, I think, the tordo, which means nothing to me and would mean something to a Florentine who knew the family. I do not know the family. I break the seal. The handwriting is good Florentine merchant’s hand, schooled but not professional, written by a man who can write his own letters and prefers to.

Maestro Leonardo,

I write to beg your assistance in a matter most unusual. My wife Lisa is afflicted by a thing no physician will name. I would set the whole truth on this page, Maestro, but if I wrote it plainly no sane man would come, and I find that I need a man who will come. The physicians bring tinctures. She drinks them. She smiles to thank them. She does not improve. She smiles, Maestro. She has smiled at every physician who has crossed my threshold. The smile is on her face when I leave the house and the smile is on her face when I return. She smiles in her sleep. She smiles as I write this, in the room across from this one, where she sits up against her pillows and looks at the wall.

The smile is not her smile.

I would not write to a maestro of your reputation for so small a thing as a wife’s illness, if I had not heard, from a friend, that you have closed doors of the kind that are not doors. The friend would not say more. He said you would understand the phrase. He said to write to you. He said you would not laugh at the letter.

I do not laugh, Maestro. I do not know how to laugh at this. My wife is sitting in the next room smiling, and the smile is not hers.

Come to my house. See her. Tell me if there is anything that can be done.

Your humble servant, Francesco del Giocondo.

I fold the letter. I do not laugh at the letter. I set it on the table beside the compass that has failed four times today to draw a circle.

The friend who told the merchant about closing doors of the kind that are not doors did not get the phrase from me. I have spoken it to no one. The friend got it from someone with a keeper’s knowledge. Someone outside my family knows my name now. They will keep knowing. The work has been a small private thing in my family for as long as I can trace; the work is no longer small or private. Someone has spoken.

“Salaino.”

“Maestro.”

“A summons.”

“From where.”

“From here. Florence.”

“From whom.”

“A merchant. His wife.”

He turns from the window.

“Sick.”

“Yes.”

“The kind we know about.”

“Yes.”

“The smile.”

“The smile.”

He has heard it in my voice before I have read him the line. He has known the line for years now, since the morning we left Milan with the box and the wrapped panel and three changes of linen. He has been waiting, perhaps, for a line like this one.

“Then we go,” he says. “Of course we go.”

“There is one thing first.”

“What.”

“The chest.”

“Ah.”

I open the wooden chest where I keep correspondence I do not throw away. I lift the wrapped panel from beneath the topmost layer. The wrapping is the same linen Antonio used. The cord is the same country knot. I have not unwrapped this panel since the morning after the refectory.

I unwrap it now.

Her portrait. The face at peace. The eyes closed. The mouth in the small smile of a critic who had been outflanked and had chosen, for dignity, to call the outflanking a draw. The gold frame holds. Four lines of gold along the four edges. The frame is still bright.

I look at the mouth.

In the corner where the upper and lower lips meet on the right side, the gold has cracked. The crack is small. A hairline. Not even the full corner. Just at the edge.

In the cracked place, the mouth has changed.

The small smile of a critic at peace is no longer a small smile of a critic at peace. There is a new expression beginning to form in the corner of the lips, in the place where the gold has thinned. The expression has not yet arrived. The expression is the way an outline almost becomes a face.

I have seen this outline before. In the shadow on the workshop wall above the wrapped panel. In the corner pigment of the refectory after the ritual.

I have not made this expression. I painted her at peace. The peace is mostly intact. The peace has begun, in one corner, to loosen.

Salai has felt me go still.

“What.”

“She is moving.”

He waits to see if I will say more. I do not. He turns back to the window.

I rewrap the panel. I retie the cord, knotted in the country knot. I place the panel back in the chest.

I cross to the larger chest, the one I brought from Milan. I open it. My grandfather’s box is inside, where I have not opened it since the morning after the refectory.

I lift the lid.

Three working vials remain, re-waxed by my own hand: blue, red, gold. The four others are still unbroken, still emergency. The journal lies at the bottom in its oil-stained leather. The pots’ temperatures have not changed.

The gold is still cold.

I close the box. I lift it from the larger chest. I place it on the table beside the merchant’s letter. The box is heavy for its size, the same wrong weight it had on the road from Vinci. The weight has not lessened in all the years since. I had thought, perhaps, that the weight was something the box had borrowed. The weight is something the box owns.

Salai has come away from the window. He cannot see the box on the table; he can hear it.

“When do we leave?”

“Tomorrow.”

Tomorrow does not come.

What comes, an hour past dark, is a fist on the street door, and boots on my stair, and a rider in the colours of Cesare Borgia with the road still steaming off him. He does not sit. He does not take wine. He recites, the way men recite who have been made to say a thing back to their master before being trusted to carry it: the Duke Valentino requires his engineer. The fortresses of the Romagna will not survey themselves. I am to come at once, with my instruments. The word requires belongs to a man who owns other words and does not use them.

I am fifty years old this month. I have a wall in Milan that is already beginning to shed its paint, a bound thing in a chest that has started, in one cracked corner, to smile, and now a letter on my table from a merchant whose wife smiles and does not stop. And I am to spend my spring drawing the killing angles of other men’s walls, because a keeper who ends on a prince’s gallows keeps nothing.

Salai does not ask. He hears the boots go down the stair and begins, without a word, to pack the instruments.

I take the merchant’s letter from the table. I read it once more, the smile that is not her smile, the friend who knows what no friend should know. Someone baits this hook, and casts it into my one clear pool, and waits. When I come to Florence, and I will come, it will be to take the hook in my hand and follow the line back to the man who tied it.

I lift the lid of my grandfather’s box. I lay the letter on top of the journal, where the important unanswered things are kept.

Forgive me, Ser Francesco. Forgive me, Madonna Lisa, whoever is wearing you.

The work is never over. The work is only postponed, and postponement is a debt, and the debt is always collected.

I close the box.

chapters.title: THE PIGMENTS WERE ONLY THE BEGINNING AN EXCLUSIVE PREVIEW OF BOOK ONE: THE MONA LISA CAGE
chapters.content:
THE PIGMENTS WERE ONLY THE BEGINNING AN EXCLUSIVE PREVIEW OF BOOK ONE: THE MONA LISA CAGE

Some faces refuse to be painted because they are not faces at all. They are doors wearing the shape of features.

Antonio da Vinci, sealed journals

Leonardo da Vinci

Milan, Santa Maria delle Grazie

February 1497

The face of Judas Iscariot has defeated me for the seventeenth time.

I stand in the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie with my brush a hand’s breadth from the wall, and I watch the empty place where the betrayer must sit. The afternoon light falls through the high windows at an angle I measured to the degree three years ago and have not needed to measure since. It lays my half-finished apostles in their proper shadow. It finds, without fail, the one patch of plaster I cannot fill.

I prepared that patch myself this morning. Slaked lime and the fine grey ash they dig at Pozzuoli, worked to the smoothness of skin. Other men race wet plaster and let the wall dictate their hours. I will not be hurried by a wall. I have devised my own ground, my own slow oils, a method I am certain will outlast the fashion of fresco and hold my colours true long after I am dust. I am certain of it the way I am certain of arithmetic. That certainty is the first thing in this room that will betray me, though I do not know it yet.

The surface is perfect. Smooth. Ready.

And it is watching me.

Madness. Six nights without proper sleep, and now I credit a wall with intentions.

I bring my hand forward. The bristle touches plaster, and I draw it down in what should be the curve of a cheekbone, the simplest stroke a child could manage, a line I have set down ten thousand times. The pigment goes wrong under my hand. Not the weight I ground into it, not the ochre I warmed with a breath of vermilion. The stroke bends where I will it straight. It thickens where I bear down light. It leaves on the wall a mark that belongs to no face I have ever studied, and I have opened the skin of the dead to learn how a face is hung upon its bone.

I step back. At the edge of my sight the mark slides, the way a fish turns under the surface of a pond. I look at it square and it is only a smear of earth and oil, still and stupid and mine. I look away, and it moves.

There. Again.

A rational man would name it the failing of a tired eye. I am a rational man. I have spent my life chasing the causes that other men hand to God or the Devil because the labour of looking is too much for them. I have cut muscle from bone by candle to see how the arm is rigged. I have watched the kite ride the wind to learn how weight makes peace with air. I have observed and measured and set down what I found, brick upon brick, until I built myself a house of reasons I believed would shelter me from anything.

And I cannot tell you what the blank space is doing.

My hand shakes. The brush jumps. A spray of ochre crosses the fresh plaster, and for the space of one heartbeat the spatter holds a shape, a wide and grinning mouth, before I drag my rag across it and it is gone.

The wall takes the correction without complaint. It returns to its smooth waiting, to that patient emptiness that has thrown down every figure I have raised against it.

Seventeen tries. The first was only poor work. I had meant a Judas of shadow and guilt, the treachery plain in the set of the brow, and what dried on the wall overnight was not the man I painted but something arranged where he had been, less a face than a hole worn into the shape of one. I scraped it back. The next was worse, and the next worse than that, each ruin further from any human grammar, until the morning my hand moved without me.

I do not remember painting the third. I remember the grey light. I remember loading the brush with burnt sienna and lead white. Then a torn place in the day, a page gone from the book, and awareness returning with my breakfast climbing my throat and a thing on the plaster no living hand should have been able to lay there. I would not look at it straight. I took it only at the edge of my eye as I scrubbed it away, and even so it has not left me: a face that was also a doorway, an eye that was also a mouth, teeth crowded where no jaw could hold them.

The prior found me an hour after, on my knees, washing sick from the refectory stones with my own sleeve.

That was months ago. Nothing since has improved my Judas.

A tread on the stones behind me now, soft, deliberate, and the small dry click of beads. I do not turn. I know the rhythm of those sandals the way a condemned man knows the bell that counts his mornings.

“The Duke grows impatient, Maestro.” Prior Bandello comes to my shoulder and folds his hands, the rosary moving through his fingers one bead at a time. He is a small man with mild eyes and a stillness that costs him effort, and I have learned to mistrust the courtesy in him precisely because it never slips. “Three years. Three years of paint and scaffolding, and a wall that is twelve parts finished and one part empty. The brothers have begun to take their meals looking at the empty part.”

“Masterworks are not hurried.”

“Masterworks are not abandoned in the middle, either.” Another bead. The click of it is very loud in the long room. “Ludovico asks after you. Daily, now. He has begun to use a word I do not enjoy carrying across the city to you.” He pauses, to be sure I will ask, and when I do not, he gives it to me anyway. “Unwell. He fears you are unwell.”

The word settles between us and does not lift.

In another man’s mouth it would mean a fever, a week abed, a physician with his jars of leeches. In Ludovico Sforza’s court it has a wider reach. It can mean a weakness that wants correcting. It can mean a madness that wants a locked room and a strong door. A duke who has paid three years of a painter’s keep and has a bare wall to show his guests will eventually decide which meaning suits his purse.

“I am perfectly well,” I tell him. “I labour at a problem of method. Nothing more.”

“What problem of method consumes three years?”

The kind that watches from the gaps in a man’s work. The kind that paints itself while I sleep on my feet. The kind that has begun to follow me home, that waits in the black of a basin when I try to wash the turpentine from my hands and looks up at me out of the water.

“The face of Judas,” I say. “I cannot find the living man who carries the particular quality I need. I have searched for him in every quarter of Milan.”

That much is not a lie. I have hunted that face through the prisons and the dockside taverns and the fine rooms where worse men than dock thieves take their wine. The merchant who sold his own brother to the debt-collectors. The courtier whose whispers emptied a rival’s house. The priest with the wife of a wool-trader warming his bed. Each of them sat for me. Each of them gave me a study in greed or cowardice or appetite, and not one of them gave me what I found in my seventeenth ruin.

Not one of them was hungry in the way the wall is hungry.

“I shall pray you find him soon.” Bandello inclines his head, and the beads go still in his hand, and for a moment the mildness in him thins to something that has measured me and is keeping the sum to itself. “Before the Duke finds his own use for the word.”

He withdraws. His sandals carry the sound of him down the length of the refectory and out, and I am left with my eleven apostles in their failing light and the empty place that no longer feels like an absence. An absence is a nothing. This has begun to feel like a held breath.

That was four hours past. I have not moved.

The light has gone from gold to amber to the deep bruised violet that comes before the dark. The shadows have stretched from the windows and reached across the floor like fingers feeling toward the wall. At the centre of my composition the Christ keeps his arms open in the gesture I built the whole table to carry. Peter still grips his small bright knife. John still sways toward sleep. Thomas still lifts the one raised finger of his doubt.

And Judas is still nothing. A void with an edge to it. A man-shaped wound in my three years’ work.

Go. The brothers will want the room for vespers. Gather your brushes and your pots and go home and come back at dawn with a rested eye and a steadier hand.

I do not go. I cannot take my eyes from the empty place, and not because I wish to look at it. Because I have become afraid of what it may do the moment I stop.

The smell comes first.

It comes from nowhere, out of no jar I have opened and no corner I can name. Paint and plaster and the clean nutty oil of linseed, the honest furniture of my craft. Then, beneath that, the other thing. Meat kept too long in summer. Cut flowers left to soften in their own water. A sweetness laid over rot to hide it, and failing, and somehow worse for the failing.

I know the smell of death. I have spent whole nights with the opened dead, reading the architecture under the skin by a guttering wick while the stink watered my eyes. That smell was honest. It was only flesh going back to the earth that lent it, the plain arithmetic of decay.

This smell is not honest. This smell intends something.

Leave. Leave now. Whatever moves in this room, you will not meet it alone and in the dark.

The counsel is good. My feet will not take it. I stand rooted on the cold stone, my eyes fixed where Judas is not, and I watch my painting begin to change.

The faces of the apostles are moving.

Peter’s honest fury loosens at its edges, the features running like colour caught in rain. The grief in John slides toward something less clean, a sweetness gone sly. And Thomas, my doubting Thomas, his one raised finger curls slowly inward, past questioning, into a hook, into a thing made not to ask but to take hold.

The empty place grows wider.

Not larger. Wider. As a mouth widens. As if the wall has begun to gape, to draw in the long table and the open-armed Christ and every figure I have raised in three years of labour, and as if all that labour were never a supper at all but only the long careful laying of a meal.

I stumble back. My heel finds a loose stone and I go down hard, my palms skidding on grit and the dust of centuries, the breath knocked white out of me. On the table the candles I keep for the close work gutter and leap, and the shadows of the apostles lurch up the walls and do not move as the flames move, do not move as shadows are bound by every law I have ever proven to move.

And in the empty place, something pushes through.

Not the sly ripple I might have laid at the door of a tired eye. This has form. This has weight. A shape pressing against the inner face of my painting from the far side, the way a hand presses into wet cloth and the cloth takes the print of every finger, the way a drowned face rises pale under still water before it breaks the surface. Something vast leaning its whole patience against a door that was never built to open.

Run.

I am on my feet without the memory of rising. I do not gather my brushes. I do not stop the pots or pinch the wicks. I do not look back to learn what wears the wall now.

I run.

The refectory door bangs wide before me and the night air takes my face like a hand laid in blessing, cold and clean and empty of that rot-sweet wrongness. I cross the cloister with my heart slamming, past the chapel where the brothers are gathering their voices for vespers, out through the gate and into the street, and Milan closes over me like water over a dropped stone. Hawkers crying the last of their wares before the dark. Servants bent under the day’s marketing. A dog at a bone, a child at a grievance, the whole loud ordinary commerce of the living, none of it knowing that something has begun to wake behind the wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie.

I do not stop until the Corte Vecchia.

My workshop holds three rooms on the upper floor of a house that has outlived its best years. The stairs complain under me, each in its own register, a music I usually find friendly and tonight hear as warning. The door sticks in its frame as it always sticks in the wet months, and I shoulder it, and it gives, and the familiar world receives me. Warmth. The amber of candles in their sconces. The smell of turpentine over everything like a benediction. Sketches pinned to every surface that will take a pin. Clay studies furred with dust on shelves I built too high to dust. Drawings of engines spread across the long table like the plans for a siege. In the corner the portrait of a councillor’s wife who paid her deposit before the autumn and will go to her grave without her likeness, because I have not been able to look at a blank panel these three years without the panel looking back.

And at the centre of the long table, between the diagram of a flooded moat and the little bronze model of a horse that will never be cast, the box sits where it has sat for two days, and where I go on pretending, for two days now, that I do not feel it watching the room.

Old wood, dark with the oil of long handling. A lid sealed with red wax, broken now, resealed by my own clumsy thumb. And pressed into the older wax, sharp after thirty years, a mark I know before my mind consents to know it.

A brush crossed with a quill. Seven stars set in a ring.

My grandfather’s seal.

It comes to me the long way, as everything true comes. A letter from my father begins it, Ser Piero, notary of Florence, a man who has not written to me in six years and who writes now in the small deliberate hand of a man who charges by the legal phrase: the chest your grandfather left in my keeping has altered, there is frost on the wax in a warm room, come and take this thing out of my house. So I go. Four days on winter roads to Vinci, and I stand in the February rain over a grave whose stone has gone soft-edged with thirty years of weather. Antonio da Vinci has lain in that churchyard since I was a boy of twelve. I held the cord they lowered him by, the autumn the leaves came down the colour of old coins, and I understand only now that the family was burying more than a man. My father will not hand the box over under his own roof. He gives it to me on the road outside the town, wrapped and corded, and says only that it goes to me and to no one else, and that I am not to write to him of it again. Four days back. The cart is in the stable. The driver is paid.

And for two days I circle this table the way a dog circles a snake it has already been bitten by.

We open it the first evening, Salai and I, by lamplight, layer by layer, saying very little. Seven sealed pots of pigment, each stopped with wax and marked in my grandfather’s hand: three set apart for use, their seals scored with a single line, and four bound over in lead, which the journal names emergency and instructs me, twice, in a script pressed hard enough to furrow the page, never to open while another road remains. Beneath the pots, the journal itself, small, leather-bound, oil-stained at the corners, with a loose page folded on top and addressed to me. Beneath everything, wrapped in linen and tied with the country knot he taught me at six, a panel the size of my two palms.

I do not read the loose page aloud, not that evening. Salai watches me fold it away and has the grace, or the cunning, not to ask.

Tonight he is out in the rain, at whatever it is he does in the rain, and I am alone with the box, and I take the page out again, because a man returns to a wound to learn whether it is healing.

Leonardo,

If this is in your hands, the signs have come, and you have lived through their coming. That is more than I dared promise myself.

I have little time and less ink for it. The thing I spent my life containing is patient past any human measure, and it waits for men like us. It feels every stroke we set down, the way a spider feels a thread go taut. You have the gift. I saw it in you at seven, in your hungry eyes. That hunger is what makes us dangerous to it, and it dangerous to you.

The pots hold pigments mixed by a method older than Rome. They will seal what nothing else will touch. Three you may spend. Four you must not, save at the last need of all. They exact a price, and the price is never the one you brace for.

The journal is the shadow of what I knew. The body of it is in Vinci, in my workshop, what the fire spared. I burned more than I should have. I was afraid of what a book can do in the wrong hands, and at the end I could no longer tell whether yours would be the right ones. Forgive me that. You will have to find the rest the way I found it.

There is more I should tell you and cannot, not on a page. When you have read this, unwrap the panel. Speak to the portrait. Make her tell you what I am no longer here to say. She will not want to. Compel her.

I am sorry the burden falls to you. I could not break the thing, only hold it, and a held thing is only ever borrowed time.

Close the doors, grandson.

With a love the grave does not lessen,

Antonio

Two days I obey every line of that letter but the one it took the most courage to write.

I lift the wrapped panel from the bottom of the box. The linen is cold. The cord is knotted in the country knot, the kind that does not slip even when the carried thing is carried by a child too small to be careful. I untie it the way he taught me, and the linen falls away, and I turn the panel over.

A portrait no bigger than my palm. A woman I have never seen.

The letter slips from my fingers. I watch it settle to the stone, his words coming to rest like leaves on the skin of a still pond.

Speak to the portrait.

I look at the small painting in my hands. The woman regards me from her frame, her eyes catching the candlelight and keeping it. Her features are pleasant and forgettable, a face that would empty from memory the moment it left a room. Brown hair under a plain veil. Pale skin. A mouth set in an expression that lives between a smile and something the smile is drawn over.

She looks hungry.

Foolishness. She is earth and oil on a board. She cannot look like anything.

Even as I frame the denial, the eyes in the portrait move. A small thing, a sliding I might lay at the door of the candle’s wavering or my own worn sight. The painted pupils track left. Then right. Then they settle on me, and hold, with an attention that lifts the hair along my arms.

“You took your time,” the portrait says.

I am against the workbench before I know I have moved. My hip strikes the edge and the pain of it flares up through my side, sharp and honest, the only honest thing in the room.

“I have waited a long while.” The lips of the painted woman do not stir. The voice rises out of the board itself, out of the wood and the colour and the varnish, as though the materials have between them learned the trick of speech. “He set me here before you were a man grown. He said you would come to it in your own time. He said the signs would show and the box would be carried and you would stand before me wearing the very face he wore the first night I spoke to him. He was right in every particular. He usually was.”

I am asleep. I dropped at last in the refectory, six nights unrested, and now I dream of speaking boards.

“You are not asleep.” Something close to amusement moves under the voice. “Though I grant you the comfort of the thought. It is easier to credit a dream than a door. Easier to wave off an impossible voice than to admit the world is wider and stranger than the house of reasons you have built to live in.”

I make myself look at her as I would look at any panel set before me for appraisal. Not at the thing she claims to be. At the work. The hand that laid her down. This is the discipline of my whole life and the only wall I have left to put at my back.

The painting is no masterwork. The drawing is sound and the modelling careful, the work of a competent journeyman who would never trouble the great names, the kind of likeness that hangs in a merchant’s hall to prove he once had money. The woman is rendered with skill and no fire.

And yet the thing disturbs me past my power to say why. The proportions are wrong, but wrong along directions I cannot lay a rule against. The space inside the frame shifts when I shift, the painted eyes coming with me past every trick I know for fixing a gaze upon a viewer. At the edge of sight the brushwork crawls, the strokes rearranging into figures that form and break apart like a thought I almost have and lose.

“What are you?”

“I am what waits on the far side. Or a piece of it. A splinter driven off the whole.” The voice does not hurry. “Your grandfather took me thirty years ago, when I came too near a door he was painting. He bound me into this board by a method I had not met before and have not met since. I would dearly like to know how he did it. He would never say.”

“What do you want?”

“What every hunger wants. To take in. To grow by it. To become larger than I was.” A pause that has weight. “But he bound me well. I cannot reach for anything without the leave of the hand that bound me, and that hand is thirty years in the ground, so its refusal has become a thing without end. You may imagine how that sits with me.”

“Then why answer me at all?”

“Because he made me.” For the first time something like temper threads the voice, dark and dry. “It is written into the binding. When the one who holds this board compels me, I must answer, and answer true. I find it a tiresome leash. I will give you the words and not one grain more than the words require, so put your questions well. A poorly asked question earns a true answer that helps you not at all.”

I lift the portrait from its linen. The frame is cold against my palms, colder than wood has any right to be on a night with a fire on the hearth, a cold that climbs my wrists and sets my teeth on edge. The painted eyes follow me as I turn her to the light and back.

“You say a splinter. A splinter of what?”

“Of the hunger behind the doors. The appetite that lives in the gap between the thing painted and the thing itself.” A silence, and under it the suggestion of vastness, the way a single dropped stone tells you the depth of a well. “We have no name your mouth could shape. We have no form your mind could hold and stay whole. Leave the names to your grandfather’s books. They will frighten you better than I can.”

“And the door he painted. You came at that.”

“He was good, the old man. Better than most who ever lifted a brush. When he painted, he painted true, and truth is the danger. Truth thins the wall. Truth wears the seam.” The voice changes, and what enters it is worse than menace, because it is admiration. “You are better than he was. I can taste it on the air of this room. I can see how the light leans toward your hands when you reach for a brush. There has not been a danger like you in a very long age. You are the most dangerous man alive, and you have spent three years widening a door with your own skill and calling it a failure to finish a face.”

The cold reaches into my chest and sits there. It is not fear, or not only fear. It is nearer to recognition, and that is the part I cannot bear.

“The empty place in the refectory,” I say. “Where Judas will not come. That is a door.”

“You have been painting one for three years and grieving that you could not. Every stroke you set there opens it a finger wider. Every Judas you raise and scrape away wears the seam thinner. It is nearly wide enough now. You felt it tonight. You felt the first of it lean through.”

“I felt something press against the wall.”

“A tendril. One blind finger put through to test the air.” The painted mouth does not move and still I know it has changed. “When the door stands open, what comes will not be a finger.”

The candles drop low all at once, as if a breath had crossed the room, and in the failing light I see them at the edges of things. Shapes that are not furniture. Faces that hold their lines only so long as I do not turn to them. Mouths opening on a black with no floor to it. Then the wicks recover, the flames stand up gold and ordinary, and I am alone with a board and a dead man’s letter on the floor.

“How is it closed?” My voice holds steady. I take some small foolish pride in that. “The door. How do I seal it before the rest comes through?”

“The pigments. He spent the back half of his life perfecting them. They bind. They seal. They shut a door that common paint slides off.”

I look at the three pots he marked for use. The wax on them is broken since the first evening, enough to see and no more. The first holds a colour that turns between red and gold and, at a certain tilt, the dark of dried blood. The second is blue gone to black gone to silver, the blue of deep water or of the last sky before dawn. The third gives off a light of its own, white and silver and gold together, like the moon run to liquid and poured into glass.

“How are they used?”

“That I cannot tell you.”

“You said you must answer true.”

“I must answer true. I cannot answer what was never given to me. He bound me with these colours. He never taught me the binding. I have felt what they do from the wrong side of it, which has taught me to fear them and nothing more.”

Wonderful. A magic with no instruction and a teacher who was

“There are notes.” The voice cuts across the thought as though it hears it, and perhaps it does. “The book he sent you is the shadow. He tells you so himself, on his page. The body of it is in Vinci, in his workshop, what he learned of the shutting of doors, the part the fire spared.” A pause, and the pleasure in it is unmistakable. “Three days’ hard riding, I believe. Such a long way, and the wall thinning by the hour. I do wonder which will arrive first. You at the notes, or the thing at you.”

“You would have me ride three days and leave the door to widen behind me.”

“I would have you do nothing. I am past wanting, remember. I merely observe that you have two roads and no good one. Ride, and pray the door is patient. Stay, and face it with colours you do not know how to spend and the shadow of a book whose body was half given to the fire.” The painted mouth does not move, and still I feel it smile. “I confess I am curious to see which you choose. It has been a long time since anything was curious to me.”

The workshop door bursts open.

I spin with the vial raised like a blade, my body falling of its own accord into a guard I did not know my muscles remembered. The figure in the doorway freezes with one hand on the frame, dark eyes gone wide.

Salai.

He is soaked. The rain runs from his hair down the sharp young planes of his face and off his jaw, and his thin shirt clings to him, and his boots leave dark prints on boards I swept three days past and will sweep again tomorrow. He squints into the room, into the candlelight, and rubs at one eye with the heel of his hand as though the brightness troubles him, though my candles are low and the room is more shadow than light.

“You’re home.” The innocence in his voice is a coat thrown over something he would rather I did not see. “I didn’t look for you so early.”

“It is near midnight.”

“Is it.” He makes a show of consulting the black windows, as if the dark out there might have lied to him. “The hours got away from me.”

Seventeen years old, and seven of them under my roof, since the morning his father brought him to me at ten with the broken hope that I might make of him something other than a thief. I have failed at that as completely as a man can fail. Salai steals what is not nailed down and a fair portion of what is. He lies with the ease of a poet and the open face of a saint. He has cost me more in replaced silver and quieted constables than most men spend on a household entire.

He is also the one soul in Milan I trust without floor or limit.

“What’s that?” He is already crossing the room, already reaching, the old thieving instinct running ahead of his sense, his eyes on the vial in my hand. He puts his face close to it and frowns, and tilts it, and frowns harder, and I see him misjudge the distance and pull his fingers back a hair too late, brushing the cold glass he had meant to pinch clean.

“Do not touch it.”

Something in the way I say it stops him, not the words, which he would shrug off, but whatever rides beneath them. The fear I cannot wholly keep down.

The careless mischief drains out of his face. What it leaves is the thing under the boy, the quick hard intelligence, the loyalty with teeth, the readiness for violence I have seen him show exactly once, in an alley by the docks, over a man who had put a knife toward me.

“What’s happened?” He comes closer, close enough that I smell the wine and the cheap rosewater of whatever company he kept tonight. “You’ve the look of a man who’s seen the dead walk.”

I have. I am seeing it still. The board behind you wears a woman’s face that moves when I look away, and somewhere across this city a door is widening that will let in a thing worse than any devil the Church has put a name to.

“Sit,” I tell him. “I have a thing to tell you, and you are going to have to believe it.”

He sits. He listens. And when I have laid it all out, the empty place and the running faces and the box with the dead man’s seal and the board that answers when it is asked, he does the one thing I did not expect.

He takes up the portrait and looks at it.

“She’s not moving now,” he says. “She’s only a painting. A poor one, if you want the truth, no offence to your grandfather.” He brings it nearer his face and squints again, and turns it toward the candle to find the light, the way a man does when the light has begun, lately, to fail him. “Plain little thing.”

“She moved before. She spoke.”

“I believe you.” He says it too quickly, and then is quiet a moment, and I watch the belief cost him. He has spent seven years arranging the world into things that can be picked up, sold, outrun, or talked past, and I have just handed him one that fits no pocket and answers no lie. His throat works. When he speaks again the bravado has thinned to something nearer the truth. “I have seen what you can do with a brush, Maestro. If you tell me a painting spoke to you, then a painting spoke. God help us both.” He sets her down, face to the ceiling, and meets my eyes, and there is no laughter left in his. “What do we do?”

“We?”

“You think I’ll stand by and let you walk into this alone?” His jaw sets. The rain has flattened his hair to his brow and made him young again, near the boy who first came through my door with defiance in his look and another man’s purse already in his sleeve. “Seven years, Maestro. Seven years of your ruin and your genius and your mad impossible schemes. You think I leave now, when at last it gets interesting?”

“This is not interesting. This is deadly.”

“With you those have never been two different things.” He rises, the water still running off him, and goes to the window. Below, Milan lies under the rain, a city of small troubles and small mercies, with no notion of what has woken three streets and a churchyard away. “What did she tell you. About the shutting of the door.”

“That I must use the colours my grandfather left. But she cannot tell me how.”

“Then we find out how.” He turns back, and his dark eyes hold the stubbornness that has kept him at my side through every scandal and every triumph and the long grey stretches between. “We go tonight. We take the colours. We try.”

“We may die. We may come to something a great deal worse than dying.”

“We may also win.” The grin breaks across him sudden and sharp, the look of a man who has staked his neck on longer odds and walked away counting his winnings. “When have you ever turned your back on a thing because you did not understand it? When have you refused to put your hand in the fire to see how the fire is made?”

Never. The answer is never, and we both know it. From the opened dead to the engines I draw that no foundry will pour, I have gone wherever the question led, and never once asked the price at the door.

But this is not natural philosophy. This is not the pushing back of ignorance one hard-won span at a time. This is the thing my grandfather gave his life to, and could not kill, and in the end could only cage.

And yet.

The door is opening. Whether I face it tonight, or run for Vinci, or bar myself in this workshop until the thing leans through and finds me anyway, the door is opening, and my hand opened it. My gift widened it. The skill that is the truest thing about me has been, these three years, a key turning slowly in a lock I never saw.

If any man can shut it, I can.

If any man must, then it is I.

“Very well.” I set the vial down among its fellows. “We go tonight. But you stay at my back. You do nothing I have not told you to do. And if it takes me, if I fall, or fail, or stand up wearing something that is no longer Leonardo, you will not try to save me. You will run, and you will not stop until Vinci, and you will find what survives of his notes, and you will learn to fight this without me.”

“I’m not going to stand there and watch you.”

“Promise me.” I turn full on him, and whatever he reads in my face cuts the rest off in his throat. “Promise me, Salai. Or I go alone and bar the door behind me.”

The silence draws out. The rain drums the glass. Somewhere off in the dark a dog gives tongue at shadows only it can see.

“I promise,” he says at last, and the words come out of him the way a tooth comes out of the jaw.

He is lying.

I know he is lying. Salai has never in his life kept a promise that stood in the way of a thing he wanted, and what he wants is to not lose me. The lie comforts me past all reason. It tells me I am not so alone as I have spent my life believing.

Dangerous. Love is the most dangerous of all the colours. It opens a seam in a man that any enemy with eyes can find.

But I cannot send him from me. I have tried, across the years, to push him toward some safer life, one with no speaking boards in it and no inheritance of dread. He will not go. He never goes.

Some doors will not close.

“Then come,” I say. “Before I remember how to be a sensible man.”

We leave the portrait where she lies. I will not carry a bound hunger toward a door that is already opening, however much she knows. Whatever waits in the refectory may be her kin, and I have read enough of my grandfather’s letter to guess what two such things might say to one another if I were fool enough to bring them within a wall’s breadth. She does not protest. She only watches us out of those painted eyes that see further than paint was ever meant to see. The letter I fold small and slide into my doublet, against the breast, over the heart. The three pots I wrap and settle in a leather pouch and hang at my belt, where I can feel their cold through the leather and through my clothes and, I half believe, through the skin beneath.

The rain has stopped. The streets still run with it, the puddles holding the broken light of the few torches that burn outside a tavern door or a rich man’s gate. Milan at midnight is no friend to a walker. Thieves work the alleys. The watch patrols the wide ways with a keener interest in a bribe than in any citizen’s throat. There is danger in every black mouth of every close.

None of it touches me tonight. I have seen what waits in the empty place. After that, a cutpurse with a knife is a thing to walk past.

We move through the city without speaking. Salai knows these streets in his blood, which alley turns blind and which gives onto a yard, which corner hides a man and which roof carries him to the next street if the running starts. He leads me by ways I would never find. Past the shuttered stalls of the Mercato, where the day’s fish has left its ghost on the cold air. Under an arch where a beggar sleeps sitting up, his breath rattling, and does not wake for us. Along a canal where the water lies black and unmoving and throws back the one lit window above it, doubled, wrong, so that for a moment I cannot tell which window is the true one and which the water’s lie, and I look away before the old fear can name what else still water has begun to show me.

Twice on the way I see him put a hand to a wall to steady a step the old Salai would have taken sure-footed in full dark. Once he checks at a low step I had thought plain to any eye, his boot finding the edge a beat late, his weight catching wrong, and he curses under his breath and rubs at his eyes with the back of his wrist and walks on. I say nothing. He would not thank me for the noticing. But the cold at my belt seems to deepen, and I think of my grandfather’s hand pressed against mine, and the patterns the tremor drew, and I begin to understand that the price the colours exact may not always be drawn from the man who spends them.

The monastery sleeps. The brothers have sung their vespers and gone to their cells to dream whatever is left a man to dream after a life given over. One light burns in the whole grey pile of it, a candle in the prior’s window, where Bandello no doubt prays for the finishing of the wall that has plagued his refectory three years.

I made my own key to the garden door, years past, when I needed my painting at hours the Church frowns upon. I have used it more times than I could count, slipping in and out like a draught, working by candle while Milan believed Leonardo asleep in his bed.

The lock turns now with its old soft click, and the door gives onto the garden.

The smell takes me at the threshold.

The same smell as the afternoon, stronger now. Paint and plaster and linseed, and under it the rot that wears sweetness like a mask. I do not need to name it twice. We both know what it is.

“Do you smell that,” Salai breathes.

“Yes.”

“What is it.”

“The door. Opening.”

We cross the garden without a word between us. Rosemary and thyme drag at our legs and give up their sharp green scent into the dark, a mercy of one breath before the wrongness closes over it again. The refectory door stands ahead of us, dark wood in darker stone, a door like any door but for the thing that waits behind it.

I reach for the handle.

Salai’s hand shuts on my arm. The grip is hard, harder than I look for in a man who has spent his life dodging honest work. His face is bloodless in the thin starlight, and his eyes are wide, and in them is a thing I have not once seen in seven years.

Fear.

“Leonardo.” It is barely a breath. “There’s something on the wall.”

I look past him, through the small grille set into the door, into the black of the refectory beyond.

The empty place where Judas will not come is no longer empty.

Something has painted itself there in the hours I was gone. Something that looks back at me through the iron grille with eyes that hold their own pale light, with a smile drawn too wide for any jaw, with features I last saw an hour ago on a board no bigger than my palm in my own workshop across the sleeping city.

The same face. The bound thing’s face. The splinter my grandfather drove into a frame and chained with a method he carried to his grave.

She has a sister.

And the sister was never bound at all.

AUTHOR’S NOTE

SOME DOORS ARE NEVER FINISHED CLOSING.

Tradition holds that Leonardo lingered a long while over the face of Judas as he worked on The Last Supper, and that his prior, the real Vincenzo Bandello, grew impatient waiting for it to be finished. The wall painting really did begin to deteriorate within a few decades, because Leonardo worked in oil and tempera on dry plaster rather than in true fresco. That experiment is part of why the masterpiece was fragile almost from the day it was done.

Antonio da Vinci was a real man, Leonardo’s grandfather. His role here as a keeper, and the dates this story lends him, belong to the fiction. The keeper-lineage, the pigments, and La Famelica are mine.

Some of the work that survives in our museums, this story supposes, was not entirely the artist’s choice.

Leo Di Lux
